REASONING CHAIN SUMMARY\n\n| Node | Claim | Evidence/Derivation | Depends On |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| **R1** | The pathogen must naturally infect *C. pallidicaule* or a close congener | *P. syringae* on quinoa [4]; *P. variabilis* on *C. pallidicaule* [5] | Background knowledge |\n| **R2** | The pathogen must enable rapid experimental cycles | *P. syringae*: 24–48 h to symptoms [6]; *P. variabilis*: ≥5 d [7]; *B. cinerea*: 3–5 d [8] | R1 |\n| **R3** | The pathogen must possess molecular/genetic tools for immune dissection | *P. syringae*: >30 effectors, SATAC library, CRISPR [9–11]; *P. variabilis*: no tools; *B. cinerea*: moderate tools [12] | R1, R2 |\n| **R4** | The pathogen must permit both compatible and incompatible interactions | *P. syringae*: R-Avr system [13]; *P. variabilis*: R1–R4 factors [14]; *B. cinerea*: necrotroph, no classic ETI [12] | R3 |\n| **R5** | *P. syringae* is the best candidate satisfying R1–R4 | Synthesis: fastest (24–48 h) + richest toolkit + hemibiotrophic PTI/ETI | R1–R4 |\n| **R6** | pv. *aptata* is the most suitable pathovar based on phylogenetic proximity | Infects beet/chard (Amaranthaceae); seed-borne in quinoa [15] | R1 |\n| **R7** | Seven-pathovar screening identifies optimal pathovar within 2 weeks | Multi-dose, multi-accession factorial design with quantitative readouts; comparable protocols validated [4,16] | R5, R6 |\n| **R8** | *P. variabilis* is a warranted secondary validation pathosystem | Natural infection confirmed [5]; complements bacterial system with biotroph-specific immunity [7,17] | R5, R7 |\n\n[Research Report 2]\n# Establishing a Robust Pathosystem for *Chenopodium pallidicaule*: Model Pathogen Selection, Virulence Screening, and Pathovar Determination for Plant Immune System Deciphering\n\n---\n\n## Abstract\n\n*Chenopodium pallidicaule* (kañihua/cañihua, 2n = 2x = 18) is a halophytic grain crop of the Andes with untapped potential for climate-resilient agriculture. To accelerate its exploitation, a genetically tractable pathosystem must be established rapidly for dissecting plant immune mechanisms. This report proposes ***Pseudomonas syringae*** as the model pathogen—uniquely satisfying the requirements of formal pathovar taxonomy, exceptional genetic tools, rapid experimental turnaround, and phylogenetic plausibility of infecting *Chenopodium*. The recommended primary pathovar is ***P. syringae* pv. *aptata*** (best balance of natural Chenopodiaceae compatibility and genetic resources), with ***P. syringae* pv. *tomato* DC3000** retained as an indispensable molecular-genetics complement. A complementary oomycete pathosystem using the natural biotroph ***Peronospora variabilis*** is advocated for studying SA-dominant, haustorium-specific immunity. A detailed 4-week rapid virulence screening protocol is presented, encompassing media compositions, six-inoculation-method comparison, adapted 0–5 disease scoring scales, CFU-based bacterial growth quantification, split-plot factorial statistical design, and complete data analysis workflow. The logical experimental pathway, expected outcomes, and evidence-based justifications are provided through a layered reasoning chain (R1–R24).\n\n---\n\n## 1. Introduction and Strategic Context\n\n### 1.1 The Imperative\n\nClimate change is expanding the ranges of biotic stresses confronting crops. *Chenopodium pallidicaule*, native to the Andean altiplano at elevations of 3,500–4,200 m, is a halophytic pseudocereal with exceptional salt tolerance, drought resilience, and nutritional quality (Mangelson et al., 2019). As this crop is introduced to novel environments, it will encounter unfamiliar pathogens—or the pathogens themselves may expand their ranges. Understanding the plant immune system of *C. pallidicaule* is therefore both an immediate agricultural necessity and a valuable opportunity to discover novel resistance mechanisms shaped by the plant's unique ecological history.\n\n### 1.2 Requirements for the Model Pathosystem\n\nTo \"establish a robust pathosystem as quickly as possible\" imposes stringent criteria:\n\n| Criterion | Rationale |\n|-----------|-----------|\n| **Formal pathovar system** | The question explicitly requests pathovar determination—a taxonomic rank formally recognized for bacteria |\n| **Genetic tractability** | Enables mechanistic dissection of immune pathways through mutant analysis, effectoromics, and genome editing |\n| **Rapid establishment** | Short generation time, easy axenic culture, quick symptom development |\n| **Documented or plausible compatibility** | Must infect *C. pallidicaule* without years of host adaptation |\n| **Coverage of major immune pathways** | PTI (PAMP-triggered immunity), ETI (effector-triggered immunity), SA/JA crosstalk |\n| **Well-characterized effector repertoire** | Permits hypothesis-driven testing of immune perception mechanisms |\n| **Greenhouse/pot amenability** | Suitable for controlled-environment studies with standardized protocols |\n\n---\n\n## 2. Layered Reasoning Chain\n\n### R1 — Taxonomic Constraint Favors Bacterial Pathogens\n\n**Claim:** The term \"pathovar\" is a formally recognized infrasubspecific taxonomic rank in the International Code of Nomenclature for bacteria, fungi, and oomycetes, but in practice it is almost exclusively applied to bacteria. Among candidate plant pathogens, only *Pseudomonas syringae* possesses a well-developed, nomenclaturally valid pathovar system (>60 recognized pathovars).\n\n**Evidence:** The ISPP Standard for the Naming of Pathovars of Phytopathogenic Bacteria defines a pathovar as \"an infrasubspecific taxon differentiated on the basis of distinctive pathogenicity to one or more plant hosts.\" For fungi and oomycetes, the equivalent terms are *forma specialis* (f. sp.) and race. *Peronospora variabilis*, the natural downy mildew of Chenopodium, historically had formae speciales (f. sp. *chenopodii*, f. sp. *betae*, f. sp. *spinaciae*), but these are now treated as conspecific within *P. variabilis* (Byford, 1967; Colque-Little et al., 2021; Fondevilla et al., 2023). What remains are virulence groups (V1–V4)—phenotypic races, not formal pathovars.\n\n**Dependencies:** None (definitional).\n\n---\n\n### R2 — *Pseudomonas syringae* Is the Only Candidate Satisfying All Four Non-Negotiable Criteria\n\n**Claim:** *P. syringae* is the only plant pathogen that simultaneously offers (i) formal pathovar designations, (ii) world-class genetic tools, (iii) rapid experimental turnaround, and (iv) plausible natural compatibility with Chenopodium.\n\n**Evidence:** Comparative assessment across seven candidate pathogen groups (Table 1).\n\n**Table 1. Comparative Suitability Assessment of Candidate Model Pathogens**\n\n| Candidate | Formal Pathovar | Genetic Tools | Speed | Chenopodium Compatibility | Overall |\n|-----------|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|\n| *P. syringae* (bacterium) | ★★★★★ | A+ | A+ | A | **A** |\n| *Hyaloperonospora arabidopsidis* (oomycete) | ☆☆☆☆☆ | A+ | B | D (Brassicaceae-only) | B− |\n| *Peronospora variabilis* (oomycete) | ☆☆☆☆☆ | F | A+ | A+ | C+ |\n| *Botrytis cinerea* (fungus) | ☆☆☆☆☆ | B− | A | A | B |\n| *Colletotrichum* spp. (fungus) | ☆☆☆☆☆ | B+ | B | B+ | B |\n| *Alternaria alternata* (fungus) | ☆☆☆☆☆ | C | C | B+ | C+ |\n| *Rhizoctonia solani* (fungus) | ☆☆☆☆☆ | D | C | B | C− |\n\n**Dependencies:** R1.\n\n---\n\n### R3 — *P. syringae* Possesses Unrivalled Genetic Resources for Immune Studies\n\n**Claim:** *P. syringae* pv. *tomato* DC3000 is the most intensively studied plant-pathogenic bacterium, with a sequenced genome (6.5 Mb; Urbach et al., 2009), ~36 functional Type III effectors with known Arabidopsis targets, a complete collection of deletion polymutants (D28E, D36E, cluster-specific, coronatine-deficient), CRISPR/Cas12a genome editing protocols (Gou et al., 2025), fluorescently labeled derivatives, and the PsyTEC overexpression library (529 T3SE alleles; Martel et al., 2022).\n\n**Evidence:** See Section 5.1 for the complete effector inventory. Key characterized systems include:\n- **PTI:** Flagellin (flg22) perceived by FLS2; elf18 perceived by EFR. Both trigger MAPK cascades, ROS burst, and PR gene expression.\n- **ETI:** AvrRpt2 → RPS2; AvrRpm1 → RPM1; HopK1 → RPS4; HopA1 → RRS1-R; HopQ1-1 → unknown R in *N. benthamiana*; HopAD1 → MKK2-dependent HR.\n- **SA/JA antagonism:** Coronatine (COR) phytotoxin mimics JA-Ile, activating COI1-mediated JAZ repressor degradation and suppressing SA defenses (Brooks et al., 2004; Worley et al., 2013).\n- **T3SS:** Δ*hrcC* mutants are non-pathogenic and serve as essential avirulent controls for separating PTI from ETI.\n\n**Dependencies:** None (literature-based).\n\n---\n\n### R4 — *P. syringae* Has Documented or Highly Plausible Compatibility with Chenopodium\n\n**Claim:** *P. syringae* has been (i) formally reported on quinoa (*C. quinoa*) causing bacterial leaf spot in Colombia (Fonseca-Guerra et al., 2021); (ii) shown preliminary infectivity on lambsquarters (*C. album*) by pv. *aptata*; (iii) historically used on *C. rubrum* for pathogenicity studies (Cleary et al., 1984).\n\n**Evidence:** Fonseca-Guerra et al. (2021) reported bacterial leaf spot on quinoa in Colombia with necrotic lesions at 2–5 dpi, confirmed by MALDI-TOF MS. *P. syringae* pv. *aptata* infects sugar beet (*Beta vulgaris*, Amaranthaceae, Caryophyllales)—the same order as Chenopodiaceae—and has preliminary evidence on *C. album* (Harveson et al., 2009; Pseudos on Seed, 2025). The phylogenetic proximity makes cross-infection to *C. pallidicaule* evolutionarily plausible and experimentally testable within weeks, not years.\n\n**Dependencies:** None (literature-based).\n\n---\n\n### R5 — *P. syringae* Has the Shortest Generation Time Among All Candidate Pathogens\n\n**Claim:** *P. syringae* doubles in ~20–30 min at 28°C, enabling bulk inoculum production (10⁸–10⁹ CFU/mL) in <2 days and rapid repeat experiments.\n\n**Evidence:** Standard YEP liquid medium at 28°C, 200 rpm yields log-phase cultures (OD₆₀₀ = 0.4–0.6, ~10⁸ CFU/mL) in 12–16 h. This contrasts with *P. variabilis* (5–9 d latent period, continuous live-host maintenance every 2–3 weeks), *B. cinerea* (12–18 h hyphal growth but slower sporulation cycles), and *Colletotrichum* spp. (>2 weeks to fruiting bodies).\n\n**Dependencies:** None (biological fact).\n\n---\n\n### R6 — *Peronospora variabilis* Is the Natural Oomycete Pathogen but Is Genetically Intractable\n\n**Claim:** *P. variabilis* is confirmed to infect *C. pallidicaule* (Rollano-Peñaloza et al., 2021) and should be maintained as a complementary pathosystem, but it can never be a classical genetic model because it is an obligate biotroph.\n\n**Evidence:** *P. variabilis* cannot be cultured axenically, lacks a sequenced genome, has zero cloned effector genes, has no transformation system, and requires continuous live-host subculturing every 2–3 weeks (Rollano-Peñaloza et al., 2022; Colque-Little et al., 2021). These constraints are fundamental to obligate biotrophy and are shared by all Peronosporaceae. Research must proceed via host-side forward genetics, heterologous effector expression, and RNAi-based approaches (HIGS/SIGS).\n\n**Dependencies:** R2.\n\n---\n\n### R7 — The Two-Pronged Strategy Is Optimal\n\n**Claim:** A dual pathosystem—bacterial (primary, immediate) plus oomycete (complementary, longer-term)—provides comprehensive immune pathway coverage while mitigating the risk that either pathogen fails.\n\n**Evidence:** The bacterial prong covers PTI, ETI, SA/JA crosstalk, and hemibiotrophy with rapid turnaround. The oomycete prong covers obligate biotroph-specific SA-dominant immunity, haustorial biology, and host-jump dynamics relevant to climate change. If the bacterial pathogen fails to infect *C. pallidicaule* (unlikely but possible), the oomycete prong—already confirmed on this host—provides a guaranteed fallback.\n\n**Dependencies:** R2, R4, R6.\n\n---\n\n## 3. Proposed Model Pathogen and Justification\n\n### 3.1 Primary Model Pathogen: *Pseudomonas syringae* (Haeckel) Winslow et al. 1920\n\nThe genus *Pseudomonas syringae* is proposed as the model pathogen for *C. pallidicaule* immune system studies. This recommendation is based on the synthesis of five independent literature analyses and represents the consensus of all evaluated evidence.\n\n**Core justification (summary of R1–R5):**\n\n1. **Formal pathovar system** (R1): *P. syringae* is the only candidate with formally recognized pathovars, directly addressing the question's requirement to determine \"which the most suitable pathovar.\"\n\n2. **Unmatched genetic tools** (R3): DC3000 and related strains offer the most extensively characterized pathogen genetics in all of plant biology—sequenced genomes, T3SS mutants, individual effector knockouts, CRISPR accessibility, fluorescent tags, and a community resource base spanning decades of research.\n\n3. **Rapid establishment** (R5): From glycerol stock to inoculated plants in 2–3 weeks; from inoculation to visible symptoms in 2–5 days; from lesion to pure culture in <24 h.\n\n4. **Plausible compatibility** (R4): Documented infection of quinoa (Fonseca-Guerra et al., 2021), preliminary infectivity of pv. *aptata* on *C. album*, and historical use of *Chenopodium rubrum* in pathogenicity studies collectively establish a strong probability of compatibility.\n\n5. **Complete immune pathway coverage:** A single pathosystem engages PTI (flagellin/elf18 perception), ETI (multiple characterized Avr–R gene pairs), SA-mediated defense (early biotrophic phase), JA-mediated defense (coronatine and late necrotrophic phase), and systemic acquired resistance.\n\n### 3.2 Complementary Pathogen: *Peronospora variabilis* (Castagne) Sacc. in De Toni 1882\n\nThe natural obligate biotroph of Chenopodium downy mildew is recommended as a secondary pathosystem for studying biotroph-specific SA-dependent immunity. This system is initiated in parallel but matures over a longer (12–24 month) horizon, focusing on host-side forward genetics, transcriptomics, and effector discovery rather than classical pathogen genetics.\n\n---\n\n## 4. Determining the Most Suitable Pathovar\n\n### 4.1 Conceptual Framework\n\nIn *P. syringae*, a **pathovar** is an infrasubspecific taxon differentiated by distinctive pathogenicity to one or more plant hosts. The >60 formally recognized pathovars each possess distinct host ranges, effector repertoires, and virulence mechanisms. For *C. pallidicaule*, the \"most suitable\" pathovar must satisfy multiple weighted criteria:\n\n| Criterion | Weight | Rationale |\n|-----------|:---:|-----------|\n| Maximum virulence (AUDPC, lesion count, bacterial multiply) | 0.25 | Disease must be observable and quantifiable |\n| Reproducibility across biological replicates and growth cycles | 0.20 | Essential for reliable, publishable science |\n| Intermediate aggressiveness (progressive over 5–10 d, not rapid necrosis) | 0.15 | Allows temporal sampling of early vs. late immune responses |\n| Genetic tractability (available mutants, sequenced genome, community resources) | 0.15 | Enables mechanistic immune dissection |\n| Availability of contrasting avirulent pathovar for ETI studies | 0.10 | Required for distinguishing resistance mechanisms |\n| Agricultural relevance (prevalence in target production regions) | 0.10 | Ensures translational impact |\n\n### 4.2 Candidate Pathovar Panel\n\nBased on the literature, the following panel is proposed for initial virulence screening:\n\n| # | Pathovar/Strain | Natural Host(s) | Rationale for Inclusion | Sequenced Genome |\n|---|---|---|---|---|\n| **1** | **pv. *aptata*** (NCPPB 1148) | *Beta vulgaris* (beet, chard) | Already infects Amaranthaceae; preliminary evidence on *C. album*; phylogenetically pre-adapted | Yes (~6.0 Mb) |\n| **2** | **pv. *tomato* DC3000** (ATCC BAA-871) | Tomato, *Arabidopsis* | Best-characterized genetic tools; extensive effector toolkit; T3SS mutants available | Yes (6.5 Mb) |\n| **3** | Quinoa-adapted isolate | *C. quinoa* (Colombia) | Already adapted to Chenopodium; may represent novel pathovar | No (priority for sequencing) |\n| **4** | pv. *syringae* B728a (ATCC 19312) | Broad dicot host range | Well-studied; coronatine-negative mutants available | Yes |\n| **5** | pv. *maculicola* ES4326 (ATCC 13868) | Brassicaceae | Reported on quinoa; distinct effector profile | Yes |\n| **6** | pv. *phaseolicola* 1156B | Legumes (bean halo blight) | Different host specificity; useful for comparative studies | Yes |\n| **7** | DC3000 Δ*hrcC* (T3SS mutant) | — | Avirulent control; essential for PTI/ETI separation | Modified DC3000 |\n\n### 4.3 Predicted Ranking and Recommended Pathovar\n\nBased on the synthesis of all evidence, the predicted ranking is:\n\n**First choice: *P. syringae* pv. *aptata*** — This pathovar narrowly edges out DC3000 on the composite decision matrix for the following reasons:\n\n1. **Documented Chenopodiaceae infectivity:** pv. *aptata* is the only *P. syringae* pathovar with published evidence of infectivity on a *Chenopodium* species (*C. album*; Harveson et al., 2009). This is the strongest phylogenetic bridge to *C. pallidicaule*.\n\n2. **Phylogenetic pre-adaptation:** pv. *aptata* naturally infects *Beta vulgaris* (Amaranthaceae, Caryophyllales). *Chenopodium* is also Amaranthaceae/Caryophyllales. The pathovar has already breached the family barrier once; cross-infection to *C. pallidicaule* is evolutionarily the most parsimonious scenario.\n\n3. **Sequenced genome with characterized effectors:** The pv. *aptata* genome (~6.0 Mb) has been sequenced, and Nikolić et al. (2023) demonstrated T3SS pili formation and effector secretion under apoplast-like conditions. Known effectors include HopA1, HopA3, HopB1, HopC1, HopD1, HopE1, HopG1, HopI1, HopQ1, and HopX1—a substantial repertoire for immune studies.\n\n4. **Appropriate virulence level:** pv. *aptata* produces scorable leaf spots on beet that develop progressively over 7–14 days without causing rapid plant death, allowing temporal sampling of immune responses.\n\n5. **Agricultural relevance:** pv. *aptata* causes significant losses in beet and chard. Understanding its host range expansion into Chenopodiaceae has direct application.\n\n**Second choice (indispensable complement): *P. syringae* pv. *tomato* DC3000** — While pv. *aptata* takes the primary role for establishing disease, DC3000 is irreplaceable as the molecular genetics toolstrain. Its contributions are summarized in Table 2.\n\n**Table 2. Complementary Roles of the Two Primary Pathovars**\n\n| Function | pv. *aptata* | pv. *tomato* DC3000 |\n|----------|:---:|:---:|\n| Natural compatibility probe | ★★★ | ★★☆ |\n| PTI assays (flg22/elf18) | ★★☆ | ★★★ |\n| Effector knockout library | ★☆☆ | ★★★ |\n| CRISPR/Cas9 editing | ★★☆ | ★★★ |\n| T3SS mutants (Δ*hrcC*) | Possible | Readily available |\n| Coronatine studies (Cor⁻ mutants) | Limited | Extensive |\n| Community resources (strains, plasmids, protocols) | Sparse | Thousands of publications |\n| Host-jump evolutionary model | ★★★ | ★★☆ |\n| Fluorescently labeled strains | Not available | JRP21/23/24 (GFP/CFP/dsRED) |\n\n**Recommendation:** Deploy pv. *aptata* as the primary pathovar for establishing disease and studying host-range evolution, while systematically exploiting DC3000's molecular toolkit for mechanistic dissection of immune signaling. If the virulence screen reveals that DC3000 is substantially more virulent than pv. *aptata* on *C. pallidicaule*, promote DC3000 to primary status and relegate pv. *aptata* to the complementary role.\n\n---\n\n## 5. Rapid Virulence Screening Protocol\n\n### 5.1 Materials and Media\n\n**Bacterial culture media:**\n\n| Medium | Composition (per litre) | Use |\n|--------|------------------------|-----|\n| YEP agar | 20 g Bacto peptone, 10 g yeast extract, 15 g agar, q.s. to 1 L H₂O; pH 7.0 ± 0.2 | Primary maintenance; single-colony isolation |\n| YEP liquid | As above, without agar | Bulk inoculum production |\n| King's B (alternative) | 20 g proteose peptone, 1.5 g K₂HPO₄, 1.5 g MgSO₄·7H₂O, 10–20 g agar, q.s. to 1 L; pH 7.2 | Fluorescein pigment production for strain identification |\n\n**Antibiotics (add after autoclaving, cool to ~50°C):**\n\n| Antibiotic | Stock | Working conc. | For strain |\n|------------|-------|---------------|------------|\n| Rifampicin | 50 mg/mL H₂O | 50 µg/mL | DC3000 and other rifampicin-resistant strains |\n| Streptomycin | 100 mg/mL H₂O | 100 µg/mL | Where needed for selection |\n| Gentamycin | 50 mg/mL H₂O | 20 µg/mL | *Agrobacterium* co-infiltration experiments |\n\n**Inoculum preparation:**\n\n- Sterile 10 mM MgCl₂ (filter-sterilized, not autoclaved, to prevent precipitation)\n- Silwet L-77 surfactant (0.01% v/v; include a phytotoxicity control)\n\n**Plant growth conditions:**\n\n| Parameter | Value |\n|-----------|-------|\n| Day temperature | 22 ± 2°C |\n| Night temperature | 18 ± 2°C |\n| Photoperiod | 12 h light / 12 h dark |\n| Light intensity | 200–300 µmol·m⁻²·s⁻¹ (PPFD) |\n| Potting medium | Pasteurised loam-based compost : perlite (1:1) |\n| Humidity post-inoculation | >90% RH for 14–16 h (plastic domes or fogging) |\n\n### 5.2 Inoculation Methods\n\nFour methods are evaluated; spray inoculation is recommended as the primary method for its balance of naturalness and reproducibility.\n\n| Method | Protocol | Pros | Cons | Recommended For |\n|--------|---------|------|------|-----------------|\n| **A. Spray** | Spray to runoff with 10⁶–10⁸ CFU/mL + 0.01% Silwet; 14 h high humidity | Mimics natural infection; uniform coverage; scalable | Requires humidity control; moderate turnaround (3–7 dpi) | **Primary screening** |\n| **B. Syringe infiltration** | infiltrate abaxial leaf surface with 10⁶ CFU/mL (needleless syringe) | Bypasses epidermal barriers; rapid (2–3 dpi); precise | Wounding may confound readouts; tests only internal tissue | ETI studies; confirmatory |\n| **C. Wound + spot** | Abrade leaf (600-grit sandpaper); spot-inoculate 5 µL droplets | Simple; rapid; good for detached-leaf high-throughput | Wounding induces JA pathway; not natural | Preliminary culling |\n| **D. Vacuum infiltration** | Submerge leaves in suspension; apply vacuum (~20 inHg, 1 min) | Uniform whole-plant; efficient for many identical plants | Requires vacuum chamber; risk of tissue damage | Large-scale screens |\n\n### 5.3 Step-by-Step Procedure (4-Week Protocol)\n\n**Week 1: Plant production and pathogen procurement**\n\n| Day | Action |\n|-----|--------|\n| 1 | Surface-sterilize *C. pallidicaule* seeds (1% NaOCl, 10 min, 3× rinse with sterile water) |\n| 2 | Germinate on moist filter paper at 25°C in darkness |\n| 8 | Order *P. syringae* glycerol stocks from ATCC (DC3000 BAA-871, ES4326 13868, B728a 19312, 1156B) and/or contact authors for quinoa-adapted isolate |\n| 10 | Transplant germinated seeds (radicle down) into pasteurised potting mix |\n\n**Week 2: Bacterial culture initiation**\n\n| Day | Action |\n|-----|--------|\n| 12 | Thaw glycerol stocks; streak onto YEP agar + appropriate antibiotic; incubate 48 h at 28°C |\n| 13 | Pick single colonies into 5 mL YEP liquid + antibiotic; grow overnight (28°C, 200 rpm) |\n| 14 | Inoculate 50 mL YEP liquid + antibiotic with 1% starter; grow to OD₆₀₀ = 0.4–0.6 (12–16 h) |\n| 15 | Harvest cells (3,000 × g, 10 min, 4°C); wash 3× in sterile 10 mM MgCl₂; resuspend at 10⁵, 10⁶, 10⁷, and 10⁸ CFU/mL |\n| 15 | Verify CFU by serial dilution plating (must be done ≥48 h before use) |\n\n**Week 3: Inoculation and initial scoring**\n\n| Day | Action |\n|-----|--------|\n| 17 | **INOCULATION DAY:** Spray all treatments to runoff; immediate 14–16 h high-humidity treatment |\n| 17 | Include mock controls (10 mM MgCl₂ + 0.01% Silwet) on same bench |\n| 18 | First check at 48 hpi; record any water-soaked lesions |\n| 19 | Score at 3 dpi: 0–5 ordinal scale + % severity (ImageJ) |\n| 19 | Collect leaf discs for CFU counting at 72 hpi |\n\n**Week 4: Confirmatory scoring and CFU quantification**\n\n| Day | Action |\n|-----|--------|\n| 21 | Score at 5 dpi (peak biotrophic phase for DC3000); collect leaf discs |\n| 23 | Score at 7 dpi; final CFU sampling |\n| 25 | Final score at 9–10 dpi; calculate AUDPC |\n| 26–29 | Data analysis: CFU counts, ANOVA, cluster analysis |\n| 30 | Decision meeting: select best pathovar(s) |\n\n### 5.4 Disease Scoring Scale\n\nAdapted from Ochoa et al. (1999) and Colque-Little et al. (2021):\n\n| Score | Category | Description | Leaf Area |\n|-------|----------|-------------|-----------|\n| 0 | Resistant | No perceptible necrosis | <1% |\n| 1 | Resistant (weak compatible) | Small (<2 mm) water-soaked spots, no coalescence | 1–5% |\n| 2 | Intermediate | Multiple small (2–5 mm) necrotic lesions with chlorotic halos | 5–15% |\n| 3 | Susceptible (moderate) | Medium lesions (5–10 mm), coalescing, prominent chlorotic halo | 15–30% |\n| 4 | Susceptible (severe) | Large (>10 mm) coalescing lesions, wilting | 30–60% |\n| 5 | Highly susceptible | Total leaf necrosis, systemic appearance, plant collapse | >60% |\n\n**Disease Severity Index (DSI):**\n\n$$\\text{DSI} = \\frac{\\sum (\\text{score} \\times \\text{number of leaves at that score})}{\\text{max score} \\times \\text{total leaves assessed}} \\times 100$$\n\n**Area Under Disease Progression Curve (AUDPC):**\n\n$$\\text{AUDPC} = \\sum_{i=1}^{n-1} \\left[ \\frac{(Y_i + Y_{i+1})}{2} \\times (t_{i+1} - t_i) \\right]$$\n\nwhere $Y_i$ = disease severity (%) at time $t_i$ (days post-inoculation), and $n$ = number of observation time points.\n\n### 5.5 Bacterial Growth Quantification\n\n**Leaf disc CFU protocol (adapted from Jacob et al., 2017; Yuan et al., 2021):**\n\n1. At each time point (0, 2, 3, 5, and 7 dpi), collect three fully expanded leaves per plant.\n2. Surface-sterilize by immersion in 70% ethanol for 2 min, rinse in sterile water, blot dry.\n3. Punch four leaf discs (0.125 cm² each, total 0.5 cm²) from each leaf, avoiding major veins.\n4. Homogenize discs in 100 µL sterile 10 mM MgCl₂.\n5. Prepare 10-fold serial dilutions to 10⁻⁸.\n6. Spot-plate 10 µL from each dilution onto YEP agar + antibiotic, in duplicate.\n7. Incubate at 28°C for 30–36 h.\n8. Calculate:\n\n$$\\text{CFU/cm}^2 = \\text{Colonies counted} \\times \\text{Dilution factor} \\times 2$$\n\n(where 2 = 100 µL homogenate volume / 10 µL spot volume / 0.5 cm² area)\n\n**Key metric:** Bacterial multiply ratio = CFU/cm² at 72 hpi ÷ CFU/cm² at 0 hpi. A ratio >100 indicates virulence; a ratio <1 indicates successful host resistance.\n\n### 5.6 Statistical Design\n\n**Split-plot design in a Randomized Complete Block (RCBD):**\n\n- Whole-plot factor: Inoculation run (block) — 3–4 replicates\n- Sub-plot factor: Pathovar — randomly assigned within each block\n- Sub-sub-plot (optional): Host genotype\n\n**Full factorial array for primary screening:**\n\n| Factor | Levels | Example |\n|--------|--------|---------|\n| Pathovar | 6–8 | DC3000, ES4326, B728a, 1156B, pv. aptata, quinoa isolate |\n| Host genotype | 4–6 | Bol 1.1, Kari, plus susceptible/resistant checks |\n| Concentration | 2–3 | 10⁶, 10⁷, 10⁸ CFU/mL |\n| Replicates | 4–6 | Biological replicates (individual plants) |\n\n**Estimated total:** 6 × 4 × 2 × 4 = 192 plants (+ 24 mock controls) ≈ **216 plants**.\n\n**Statistical model:**\n\n$$Y_{ijk} = \\mu + \\alpha_i + \\beta_j + (\\alpha\\beta)_{ij} + \\epsilon_{ijk}$$\n\nwhere $\\alpha_i$ = pathovar effect, $\\beta_j$ = host genotype effect, $(\\alpha\\beta)_{ij}$ = interaction (the most biologically relevant term).\n\n**Multiple comparisons:** Dunnett's test for pathovar vs. mock; Tukey HSD for pairwise pathovar comparisons; Fisher's LSD for interaction contrasts.\n\n**Power analysis:** With a large effect size (Cohen's d = 2.0, typical for virulent vs. avirulent interactions), 4 replicates per treatment provide 80% power at α = 0.05.\n\n### 5.7 Positive and Negative Controls\n\n| Control | Expected Result | Purpose |\n|---------|----------------|---------|\n| *C. pallidicaule* + DC3000 | Water-soaked lesions at 48–72 hpi; bacterial multiply >10² at 72 hpi | Confirms susceptibility |\n| *Arabidopsis* Col-0 + DC3000 | Classic necrotic lesions; growth 10⁶→10⁹ CFU/cm² in 5 d | Validates bacterial virulence |\n| *C. pallidicaule* + mock | No lesions; normal growth | Rules out abiotic stress |\n| *C. pallidicaule* + DC3000 Δ*hrcC* | No disease; bacterial numbers decline after 48 h | Confirms T3SS requirement for virulence |\n| *Brassica nigra* + DC3000 | No lesions; bacterial death | Validates non-host status of experimental setup |\n\n### 5.8 Koch's Postulates (Pathogen Re-isolation)\n\n1. At 5–7 dpi, excise small piece of lesion margin (including healthy tissue ahead of necrotic front).\n2. Surface-sterilize by brief flaming or 70% ethanol (30 s), rinse in sterile water.\n3. Aseptically section and place on YEP agar + selective antibiotic.\n4. Incubate at 28°C for 48–72 h; observe for bacterial exudation and colony morphology.\n5. Confirm identity by Gram stain (Gram-negative rods), colony morphology, and PCR amplification of *rpoD* (~2.2 kb) followed by Sanger sequencing.\n6. Re-isolated bacterium must match the original inoculum in all characteristics.\n\n---\n\n## 6. Logical Experimental Steps for Immune System Deciphering\n\n### Phase 1: Pathosystem Establishment and Pathovar Selection (Weeks 1–8)\n\n**R8 — Pathogen Procurement and Multiplication (Weeks 1–2)**\n\n**Claim:** Reference strains of all candidate pathovars can be procured from culture collections within one week and multiplied to working stocks within two weeks.\n\n**Protocol:** Order DC3000 (ATCC BAA-871), ES4326 (ATCC 13868), B728a (ATCC 19312), 1156B (NCTC 11561), and pv. *aptata* (NCPPB 1148 or equivalent). Collect quinoa leaf samples showing bacterial leaf spot from fields in Colombia or local greenhouses; isolate *P. syringae* by single-colony isolation on selective medium. Extract genomic DNA; amplify and sequence *rpoD*, *hopO*, or *fliC* for species/pathovar confirmation. Prepare working stocks at −80°C in 15% glycerol.\n\n**Expected outcome:** 6–7 verified *P. syringae* strains, each with confirmed identity and adequate biomass for screening.\n\n**Dependencies:** R1, R4.\n\n---\n\n**R9 — Comparative Virulence Screening Identifies the Most Aggressive Pathovar (Weeks 3–5)**\n\n**Claim:** The spray inoculation protocol described in Section 5 will rank all candidate pathovars by disease severity, bacterial multiply, and reproducibility within 4 weeks.\n\n**Protocol:** Execute the 4-week screening protocol (Section 5.3). Score at 3, 5, 7, and 10 dpi. Calculate AUDPC for each pathovar × concentration combination. Perform two-way ANOVA (pathovar × host genotype). Apply the weighted decision matrix (Section 4.3) to select the primary pathovar.\n\n**Expected outcome:** \n- pv. *aptata* and/or DC3000 predicted to show highest virulence (lesions at 48–72 hpi, bacterial multiply 10²–10³ at 72 hpi)\n- Local quinoa isolate predicted to show moderate-to-high virulence\n- pv. *phaseolicola* and possibly pv. *maculicola* predicted to show lower virulence\n- At least 2–3 pathovars advancing to the refinement phase\n\n**Dependencies:** R5, R8.\n\n---\n\n**R10 — Dose-Response and Stability Refinement (Weeks 6–8)**\n\n**Claim:** The selected top pathovars must be characterized by dose-response curves and passage stability before committing to long-term studies.\n\n**Protocol:**\n1. Inoculate *C. pallidicaule* at 10⁵, 10⁶, 10⁷, and 10⁸ CFU/mL to determine ID₅₀ (effective concentration for 50% disease severity).\n2. Test infection at different developmental stages (2-leaf, 4-leaf, flowering).\n3. Pass selected pathovar through 3–5 consecutive *C. pallidicaule* plants; re-assess virulence to ensure genetic stability.\n4. Determine optimal environmental conditions (temperature 15–30°C, humidity 60–100% RH, light regime).\n\n**Expected outcome:** Optimized inoculation protocol (concentration, plant age, environmental conditions) for each selected pathovar; verified stable pathovars.\n\n**Dependencies:** R9.\n\n---\n\n### Phase 2: Immune Profiling (Weeks 9–16)\n\n**R11 — PTI Activation Assays (Weeks 9–10)**\n\n**Claim:** *C. pallidicaule* likely possesses orthologues of the canonical PTI machinery (FLS2, EFR, BAK1, BIK1, etc.), which can be activated by *P. syringae* flagellin (flg22) and elf18 peptides.\n\n**Protocol:**\n1. Treat *C. pallidicaule* leaves with synthetic flg22 peptide (1 µM) or elf18 peptide (1 µM) — available from commercial suppliers (e.g., GenScript, Biomatik).\n2. Measure ROS burst by luminol-enhanced chemiluminescence or H₂O₂-sensitive dye (CellROX).\n3. Measure MAPK phosphorylation by Western blot using phospho-specific antibodies against MPK3 and MPK6 (or cross-reactive anti-phospho-p44/p42).\n4. Measure *PR1* (SA marker), *LOX2* (JA marker), and *ERD1* (PTI marker) expression by qRT-PCR at 0, 15, 30, 60, 120, and 240 min post-treatment.\n5. Compare response to WT DC3000 vs. DC3000 Δ*fliC* (flagellin-deficient) to confirm flg22 specificity.\n\n**Expected outcome:** Detection of flg22-induced ROS burst, MAPK phosphorylation, and *PR1*/*ERD1* upregulation in *C. pallidicaule*, confirming functional PTI. If the response is weaker than in *Arabidopsis*, this may reflect differences in receptor affinity or downstream signaling—both publishable findings.\n\n**Dependencies:** R3, R10.\n\n---\n\n**R12 — ETI and Hypersensitive Response Characterization (Weeks 10–12)**\n\n**Claim:** If *C. pallidicaule* carries NLR receptors that recognize specific DC3000 Type III effectors, an incompatible interaction with HR will ensue. Even in the absence of natural R-gene recognition, systematic effector deletion can identify which effectors suppress PTI and which trigger cell death.\n\n**Protocol:**\n1. Inoculate *C. pallidicaule* with DC3000 wild-type and a panel of single-effector deletion mutants (Δ*avrPto*, Δ*avrPtoB*, Δ*hopQ1-1*, Δ*hopAD1*, Δ*hopK1*, etc.).\n2. Score HR at 48–72 hpi by trypan blue staining of leaf discs; quantify stained area by ImageJ.\n3. Measure callose deposition by aniline blue fluorescence microscopy.\n4. For each effector mutant, compare bacterial growth (CFU/cm²) to WT DC3000.\n5. If HR is observed on specific mutants, this indicates that *C. pallidicaule* recognizes the missing effector (the effector is an avirulence determinant in this host).\n\n**Expected outcome:** Identification of at least one effector whose deletion attenuates virulence or triggers HR, providing a starting point for R-gene discovery. If no HR is observed with any single mutant, this indicates that *C. pallidicaule* lacks cognate NLRs for the tested effectors—a finding that constrains future R-gene mining.\n\n**Dependencies:** R3, R11.\n\n---\n\n**R13 — Hormone Quantification (Weeks 12–14)**\n\n**Claim:** The hemibiotrophic lifestyle of DC3000 engages both SA (early biotrophic phase) and JA (late necrotrophic phase, mediated by coronatine) pathways, enabling a single pathosystem to study hormone crosstalk.\n\n**Protocol:**\n1. Sample inoculated leaves at 0, 6, 12, 24, 48, and 72 hpi.\n2. Extract hormones by methanol/water/formic acid (80:19:1, v/v/v).\n3. Quantify SA, JA, JA-Ile, IAA, ABA, and ethylene precursors by LC-MS/MS (targeted metabolomics).\n4. Compare WT DC3000 vs. DC3000 Δ*cmaL* (coronatine-deficient) to resolve COR-dependent vs. COR-independent hormone changes.\n5. Pre-treat leaves with exogenous SA (100 µM) or MeJA (50 µM) before inoculation to test priming and cross-talk.\n\n**Expected outcome:** SA peak at 12–24 hpi (PTI/ETI activation); JA peak at 6–12 hpi (wounding/COR response); SA/JA antagonism evident from reduced SA accumulation in COR-producing WT infection vs. Cor⁻ infection. These data establish the hormonal framework for all subsequent immune studies.\n\n**Dependencies:** R3, R12.\n\n---\n\n### Phase 3: Molecular Dissection (Weeks 17–24)\n\n**R14 — Transcriptomic Profiling (Weeks 17–20)**\n\n**Claim:** RNA-seq of *C. pallidicaule* leaves during infection by the selected pathovar will identify host immune genes, including orthologues of known *Arabidopsis* immunity genes and novel, lineage-specific defenses.\n\n**Protocol:**\n1. Sample leaves at 0, 6, 12, 24, 48, and 72 hpi for each pathovar (WT and Δ*hrcC*).\n2. Extract total RNA; enrich for poly-A mRNA; sequence (Illumina NovaSeq, 50M reads per sample, 3 biological replicates).\n3. Align reads to the *C. pallidicaule* reference genome (Mangelson et al., 2019; GenBank assembly GCA_000828875.2).\n4. Identify differentially expressed genes (DEGs) using DESeq2 (|log₂FC| > 2, FDR < 0.05).\n5. Annotate DEGs by GO enrichment and KEGG pathway mapping.\n6. Specifically look for orthologues of: *FLS2*, *EFR*, *BAK1*, *BIK1*, *RPM1*, *RPS2*, *RPS4*, *EDS1*, *PAD4*, *SAG101*, *NPR1*, *PR1*, *LOX2*, *COI1*, *ACS2*, *ACS4*.\n\n**Expected outcome:** A public RNA-seq dataset documenting the *C. pallidicaule* transcriptional response to bacterial infection; identification of 50–200 DEGs with known immune function; prioritization of candidate NLR genes (CC-NLR and TIR-NLR families) for functional validation.\n\n**Dependencies:** R11, R13.\n\n---\n\n**R15 — Effector Functional Validation via Agrobacterium-Mediated Transient Expression (Weeks 18–24)**\n\n**Claim:** Individual DC3000 Type III effectors can be delivered into *C. pallidicaule* cells via *Agrobacterium tumefaciens*-mediated transient expression, enabling direct testing of effector effects on host physiology.\n\n**Protocol:**\n1. Clone candidate effector genes (e.g., *avrPto*, *avrPtoB*, *hopM1*, *hopN1*, *hopA1*, *hopX1*, *corL*) into pGreenII or pCAMBIA vectors under the 35S promoter.\n2. Transform *Agrobacterium tumefaciens* strain GV3101 or AGL1.\n3. Infiltrate *A. tumefaciens* suspension (OD₆₀₀ = 0.5–1.0 in infiltration buffer: 10 mM MgCl₂, 200 µM acetosyringone, 0.01% Silwet L-77) into *C. pallidicaule* leaves (modified from Xiao et al., 2022 and Porras-Murillo et al., 2025 protocols for quinoa).\n4. Include *N. benthamiana* as a positive control (known effector interactions).\n5. Monitor at 48–72 hpi for: HR (trypan blue staining), chlorosis, cell collapse, and modulation of PTI markers (ROS, MAPK).\n\n**Expected outcome:** \n- Effectors known to suppress PTI (e.g., HopX1, HopAO1, AvrPtoB) should suppress flg22-induced ROS when co-infiltrated with flg22.\n- Effectors recognized by *N. benthamiana* NLRs (HopQ1-1, HopAD1) should trigger HR.\n- Effectors that trigger HR in *N. benthamiana* but not in *C. pallidicaule* indicate that the cognate NLR is absent from *C. pallidicaule*.\n- Effectors that trigger HR in both species indicate conserved NLR recognition.\n- Novel effectors triggering HR specifically in certain *C. pallidicaule* accessions but not others indicate accessions-specific R-genes—a starting point for R-gene cloning.\n\n**Dependencies:** R3, R14.\n\n---\n\n**R16 — VIGS-Based Gene Silencing for Functional Validation (Weeks 20–24)**\n\n**Claim:** Virus-induced gene silencing (VIGS) can be adapted for *C. pallidicaule* using the Apple latent spherical virus (ALSV) vector, which has been successfully established in quinoa (Ogata et al., 2021; Melgar et al., 2024).\n\n**Protocol:**\n1. Clone candidate *C. pallidicaule* immune gene fragments (e.g., *Fls2*, *Efr*, *Rpm1*, *Eds1*, *Npr1*, *Lox2*, *Coi1*, or novel NLR candidates from the RNA-seq) into the ALSV vector.\n2. Agroinfiltrate *C. pallidicaule* seedlings.\n3. After 2–3 weeks, challenge-inoculate with the selected *P. syringae* pathovar.\n4. Compare disease severity between VIGS and empty-vector control plants.\n5. Silencing efficiency verified by qRT-PCR.\n\n**Expected outcome:** Silencing of positive immune regulators (e.g., *Fls2*, *Eds1*) should increase susceptibility; silencing of negative regulators should increase resistance. This provides genetic validation of the transcriptomic predictions.\n\n**Dependencies:** R14, R15.\n\n---\n\n### Phase 4: Complementary Oomycete Pathosystem (Months 6–24)\n\n**R17 — *Peronospora variabilis* Isolation and Multiplication (Overlapping Months 1–3)**\n\n**Claim:** *P. variabilis* sporangia can be collected from naturally infected *C. pallidicaule* plants and multiplied on susceptible quinoa cultivar 'Real' under greenhouse conditions.\n\n**Protocol:** Based on Rollano-Peñaloza et al. (2021, 2022):\n1. Collect leaves with abundant gray-violaceous sporulation from *C. pallidicaule* (Bolivia: La Paz region, Titicaca basin; or local greenhouses).\n2. Place leaves in glass container with moist filter paper, 4°C for 2–4 h to stimulate sporangial release.\n3. Gently brush sporulating surface with soft brush into sterile distilled water.\n4. Filter through double-layer cheesecloth (50 µm); count sporangia using hemocytometer.\n5. Adjust to 1 × 10⁶ sporangia/mL in sterile water with 25 µg/mL propiconazole (prevents bacterial contamination).\n6. Spray-inoculate susceptible quinoa cv. 'Real'; maintain 24 h high-humidity at 15°C.\n7. Sub-culture every 2–3 weeks by repeating the inoculation cycle.\n\n**Expected outcome:** Established *P. variabilis* culture maintained on quinoa and *C. pallidicaule*; sporangia available for screening.\n\n**Dependencies:** R6.\n\n---\n\n**R18 — Virulence Grouping of *P. variabilis* Isolates on *C. pallidicaule* (Months 3–6)**\n\n**Claim:** *P. variabilis* isolates can be classified into existing virulence groups (V1–V4) or designated as new groups based on their compatibility profiles on a differential set of *C. pallidicaule* accessions.\n\n**Protocol:**\n1. Assemble a panel of 20–30 *C. pallidicaule* accessions from different geographic origins.\n2. Select 15–20 *P. variabilis* isolates representing different geographic origins and the known quinoa differential set (ECU-288 susceptible, ECU-291 [R1], ECU-270 [R2], ECU-379 [R3]).\n3. Inoculate each *C. pallidicaule* accession with each isolate using the spray method (1 × 10⁶ sporangia/mL, 24 h humidity at 15°C).\n4. Score at 5, 7, 9, 12, and 19 dpi on the 0–5 scale (adapted from Ochoa et al., 1999).\n5. Construct a compatibility matrix (accessions × isolates).\n6. Cluster isolates by compatibility profiles to delineate virulence groups.\n7. Test whether *C. pallidicaule* accessions carry functional orthologues of quinoa R1, R2, and R3 resistance factors.\n\n**Expected outcome:** \n- Classification of *C. pallidicaule*-isolated *P. variabilis* into existing virulence groups (most likely V4, which overcomes all known resistance factors).\n- Identification of *C. pallidicaule* accessions that show resistance (HR) to specific virulence groups—these become the resistant differential lines.\n- Possible discovery of new virulence groups if some isolates show unique compatibility profiles not matching V1–V4.\n\n**Dependencies:** R17.\n\n---\n\n**R19 — *P. variabilis* Transcriptomics and Effector Discovery (Months 6–24)**\n\n**Claim:** RNA-seq of *P. variabilis* during infection of *C. pallidicaule* will identify expressed RXLR and Crinkler effector candidates, even though the pathogen cannot be genetically manipulated.\n\n**Protocol:**\n1. Infect *C. pallidicaule* with *P. variabilis* (virulent interaction on susceptible accession).\n2. At 24, 48, 72, and 120 hpi, excise inoculated leaves showing early symptoms; surface-sterilize; freeze in liquid N₂.\n3. Extract total RNA from infected tissue.\n4. Enrich for pathogen-specific transcripts by: (a) subtractive hybridization (suppressional subtraction hybridization) against uninfected leaves; or (b) digital transcriptome subtraction using bioinformatics.\n5. Sequence the enriched fraction; assemble transcripts; predict open reading frames.\n6. Screen for canonical oomycete effector motifs: signal peptide (SignalP), RXLR-dEER motif (RXLRfinderr), and W-Y/W-F-W motifs (for Crinklers).\n7. Clone candidate effectors into pGreenII; transiently express in *C. pallidicaule* and *N. benthamiana* to test for HR elicitation, cell death suppression, or localization patterns.\n\n**Expected outcome:** Identification of 20–50 candidate RXLR/Crinkler effector genes from *P. variabilis*; functional characterization of ≥3 effectors in *C. pallidicaule*; establishment of a foundation for the *P. variabilis* effector biology program.\n\n**Dependencies:** R18.\n\n---\n\n### Phase 5: Long-Term Program Development (Months 12–24)\n\n**R20 — *P. variabilis* Genome Sequencing (Month 12 Onward)**\n\n**Claim:** De novo assembly of a high-quality *P. variabilis* reference genome using PacBio HiFi or Oxford Nanopore + Hi-C scaffolding would transform the pathosystem from transcriptome-limited to genome-enabled.\n\n**Rationale:** No *P. variabilis* genome exists. The close relative *P. effusa* (spinach downy mildew) has a 59 Mb T2T assembly with 307 predicted effectors (Fletcher et al., 2021). Given the conserved karyotype of Peronospora (17 chromosomes; Bas et al., 2023), a *P. variabilis* genome is highly achievable and would be a transformative resource for the quinoa/cañihua research community.\n\n**Dependencies:** R6, R19.\n\n---\n\n**R21 — Forward Genetics in *C. pallidicaule* (Months 12–24)**\n\n**Claim:** EMS mutagenesis of *C. pallidicaule* followed by screening for altered susceptibility to the selected *P. syringae* pathovar can identify novel host resistance genes.\n\n**Protocol:**\n1. Mutagenize *C. pallidicaule* seeds with EMS (0.2–0.5% v/v, 4–8 h) — dose optimized to achieve ~1 mutation per 10⁵ bp.\n2. Grow M₁ plants; self-pollinate; collect M₂ seeds.\n3. Plant M₂ populations (individual M₁ plants × 20 M₂ siblings each).\n4. Inoculate with the selected *P. syringae* pathovar at the 4–6 leaf stage.\n5. Screen for altered disease severity compared to unmutagenized controls.\n6. Map mutations by bulked segregant analysis (BSA) and whole-genome sequencing.\n\n**Dependencies:** R10, R11.\n\n---\n\n## 7. Expected Outcomes and Decision Points\n\n### 7.1 Summary of Expected Outcomes by Phase\n\n| Phase | Timeline | Key Deliverable | Success Metric |\n|-------|----------|-----------------|----------------|\n| 1 | Weeks 1–8 | Validated pathovar(s) | ≥2 pathovars producing reproducible disease on *C. pallidicaule* |\n| 2 | Weeks 9–16 | PTI/ETI hormone and signaling data | Flg22-induced ROS + MAPK; HR on specific effector mutants |\n| 3 | Weeks 17–24 | Transcriptome + effector functions | RNA-seq dataset; ≥3 effectors functionally characterized |\n| 4 | Months 6–24 | *P. variabilis* differential set + effectors | Classified virulence groups; ≥3 candidate effectors validated |\n| 5 | Months 12–24 | Genome + forward genetics | *P. variabilis* reference genome; EMS mutant with altered susceptibility |\n\n### 7.2 Critical Decision Points\n\n**Decision Point 1 (Week 4):** Does any *P. syringae* pathovar produce disease on *C. pallidicaule*?\n\n- **YES (predicted):** Proceed with selected pathovar(s) to Phase 2.\n- **NO (unlikely but possible):** \n  - Test wound-assisted inoculation (Method C, Section 5.3).\n  - Isolate bacteria directly from symptomatic *C. pallidicaule* plants in the field.\n  - If *C. pallidicaule* is genuinely a non-host for all *P. syringae* pathovars, pivot to *P. variabilis* as the sole primary pathosystem and invest in de novo genetic tool development (protoplast culture, PEG-mediated transformation, CRISPR delivery via *Agrobacterium*).\n\n**Decision Point 2 (Week 8):** Is pv. *aptata* or DC3000 more virulent?\n\n- **pv. *aptata* more virulent:** Maintain as primary; DC3000 as molecular complement.\n- **DC3000 more virulent:** Promote DC3000 to primary; pv. *aptata* remains for host-jump studies.\n- **Comparable:** Use pv. *aptata* as primary (better host-adaptation narrative) and DC3000 as molecular toolstrain.\n\n**Decision Point 3 (Week 12):** Does *C. pallidicaule* mount ETI (HR) against any DC3000 effector mutant?\n\n- **YES:** Identify the avirulent effector and the cognate *C. pallidicaule* NLR—this is a high-impact finding.\n- **NO:** *C. pallidicaule* lacks cognate NLRs for the tested effectors. Focus on PTI and basal resistance; explore whether *C. pallidicaule* NLRs recognize effectors from pv. *aptata* or local isolates instead.\n\n---\n\n## 8. Risk Mitigation and Contingency Planning\n\n| Risk | Probability | Impact | Mitigation |\n|------|:---:|:---:|------------|\n| No *P. syringae* pathovar infects *C. pallidicaule* | Low | High | Pivot to *P. variabilis*; isolate local bacteria from symptomatic plants; test *Botrytis cinerea* as alternative necrotroph model |\n| pv. *aptata* too aggressive (rapid plant death) | Low | Medium | Use lower inoculum (10⁵–10⁶ CFU/mL); select attenuated mutants by serial passage |\n| pv. *aptata* too mild (no symptoms) | Medium-low | Medium | Test wound inoculation; verify pathovar identity; use as avirulent control if HR-inducing |\n| DC3000 genetic tools unavailable (MTA delays) | Medium | Low | Use CRISPR/Cas12a system (Gou et al., 2025) to generate custom deletions; construct single-effectors knockouts in-house |\n| *P. variabilis* culture lost (obligate biotroph) | Medium | High | Maintain ≥3 independent parallel cultures; store infected seed as biological backup; establish cryopreservation protocol for sporangia |\n| *C. pallidicaule* shows strong basal resistance to all pathogens | Low | Medium | This would be a positive finding for a halophytic crop; characterize basal resistance mechanisms (cell wall fortification, pre-formed antimicrobials, stomatal density) as a stand-alone project |\n\n---\n\n## 9. Layered Reasoning Chain: Final Conclusions\n\n### R22 — *P. syringae* pv. *aptata* Is the Single Best Pathovar for *C. pallidicaule*\n\n**Claim:** pv. *aptata* optimally balances natural compatibility (documented on *C. album* and *Beta*), genetic resources (sequenced genome, characterized T3SS effectors), appropriate virulence for quantitative phenotyping, and agricultural relevance.\n\n**Evidence:** Synthesis of R1–R11, weighted decision matrix (Section 4.3), and comparative assessment.\n\n**Dependencies:** R1, R2, R4, R5, R10.\n\n---\n\n### R23 — DC3000 Is Indispensable as the Molecular Genetics Complement\n\n**Claim:** DC3000's unrivalled effector toolkit, T3SS mutants, CRISPR accessibility, and community resources make it essential for mechanistic immune dissection, regardless of which pathovar proves most virulent.\n\n**Evidence:** R3, Table 2.\n\n**Dependencies:** R3.\n\n---\n\n### R24 — The Two-Pronged Bacterial-Oomycete Strategy Provides Comprehensive Immune Coverage\n\n**Claim:** The combination of *P. syringae* (hemibiotroph: PTI + ETI + SA/JA crosstalk) and *P. variabilis* (obligate biotroph: SA-dominant, haustorium-specific immunity) spans the full spectrum of plant immune mechanisms while providing orthogonal validation systems.\n\n**Evidence:** R6, R7, R17–R19.\n\n**Dependencies:** R6, R7.\n\n---\n\n## 10. Summary of Recommendations\n\n| Component | Recommendation |\n|-----------|---------------|\n| **Model pathogen (genus/species)** | ***Pseudomonas syringae*** — the only pathogen combining formal pathovar system, exceptional genetic tools, rapid establishment, and plausible Chenopodium compatibility |\n| **Primary pathovar** | ***P. syringae* pv. *aptata*** — best balance of natural Chenopodiaceae compatibility, sequenced genome, characterized effectors, and agricultural relevance |\n| **Molecular-genetics complement** | ***P. syringae* pv. *tomato* DC3000** — gold-standard strain with unrivalled effector toolkit, T3SS mutants, and community resources |\n| **Avirulent control** | **DC3000 Δ*hrcC*** (T3SS-deficient) — essential for separating PTI from ETI |\n| **Complementary oomycete pathogen** | ***Peronospora variabilis*** (virulence group 4) — natural biotroph of *C. pallidicaule* for SA-dependent, haustorium-specific immunity studies |\n| **Rapid screening method** | Spray inoculation at 10⁶–10⁸ CFU/mL, 14 h high humidity, score at 3–10 dpi using adapted 0–5 scale |\n| **Key immune readouts** | ROS burst, MAPK phosphorylation, PR gene expression, HR (trypan blue), callose deposition, bacterial multiply (CFU/cm²), SA/JA quantification by LC-MS/MS |\n| **Timeline to robust pathosystem** | 8–12 weeks for basic infection protocol and first PTI/ETI data; 12–24 months for full molecular dissection |\n\n---\n\n## 11.
