EXECUTIVE SUMMARY\n\nThis report proposes the establishment of a dual-tier pathosystem in the halophytic crop *Chenopodium pallidicaule* (cañahua/cañihua; family Amaranthaceae, formerly Chenopodiaceae) to accelerate the deciphering of its plant immune system. The **primary model pathogen** is the obligate biotrophic oomycete ***Peronospora variabilis*** Gäum., the causal agent of quinoa downy mildew—this pathogen is **confirmed to naturally infect *C. pallidicaule*** under greenhouse conditions in Bolivia (Rollano-Peñaloza et al., 2021), has a short 9–11 day infection cycle, and possesses an established framework of four virulence groups (V1–V4) with corresponding resistance factors (R1–R3). The **secondary complementary pathogen** is the hemibiotrophic bacterium ***Pseudomonas syringae* pv. *aptata*** (strain P21), a natural pathogen of beet and spinach (also Amaranthaceae), offering superior genetic tractability for molecular dissection.\n\nThe **recommended pathovar (virulence group) for studying disease processes** is **V4**, the most aggressive group that overcomes resistance factors R1, R2, and R3, ensuring robust compatible interactions on the widest range of *C. pallidicaule* genotypes. For **resistance mechanism studies**, a **V1 or V2 isolate** incompatible with resistant *C. pallidicaule* accessions (e.g., cv. 'Bol 1.1') is recommended. A rapid three-tier screening pipeline—quarantine isolation → leaf-disk dose-response microassay → full-plant greenhouse confirmation—is described to quickly quantify virulence and identify the most suitable isolates within 8–12 weeks.\n\n---\n\n## 2. INTRODUCTION AND STRATEGIC RATIONALE\n\n### 2.1 The Case for *Chenopodium pallidicaule*\n\n*Chenopodium pallidicaule* Aellen (cañahua, kañawa; 2n = 2x = 18) is a semi-domesticated Andean crop highly tolerant to frost, drought, and saline soils, cultivated at 3,600–4,400 m a.s.l. in the Bolivian and Peruvian Altiplano (Mangelson et al., 2019). Its diploid genome (~363 Mbp, 22,832 annotated gene models) has been sequenced and chromosome-scale assembled, revealing strong synteny with the A-subgenome of allotetraploid quinoa (*C. quinoa*, AABB, 2n = 4x = 36). This positions *C. pallidicaule* as an **ideal simplified genetic model** for studying gene function in the Amaranthaceae. Despite its agricultural potential, the crop's immune system and disease resistance mechanisms remain profoundly understudied, representing a critical knowledge gap as climate change drives the expansion of crop cultivation into new environments where biotic stresses may intensify.\n\n### 2.2 Why a Model Pathosystem Is Needed\n\nDeciphering plant immunity requires well-characterized, genetically tractable pathosystems—reciprocal interactions between a host and its pathogen in which both partners have tools available for molecular manipulation. The plant immune system operates via two layered responses: **PAMP-triggered immunity (PTI)** at the cell surface and **effector-triggered immunity (ETI)** inside cells, often manifesting as hypersensitive response (HR) programmed cell death (Jones & Dangl, 2006). Biotrophic pathogens such as downy mildews are particularly valuable for studying these layers because they must maintain living host tissue, forcing sustained immune engagement. The *Arabidopsis*–*Hyaloperonospora arabidopsidis* pathosystem exemplifies how such systems yield deep mechanistic insights (Baxter et al., 2010).\n\n### 2.3 Objectives\n\n1. Select and justify the most suitable model pathogen for *C. pallidicaule*.\n2. Describe a rapid virulence screening protocol.\n3. Determine the most suitable pathovar (virulence group/race).\n4. Provide logical experimental steps with expected outcomes.\n\n---\n\n## 3. MODEL PATHOGEN SELECTION AND JUSTIFICATION\n\n### 3.1 Systematic Candidate Evaluation\n\nCandidates were evaluated across three pathogen kingdoms (oomycetes, bacteria, fungi) against criteria essential for rapid pathosystem establishment: (i) confirmed natural compatibility with *C. pallidicaule* or close relatives; (ii) lifestyle relevance to plant immunity (biotroph > hemibiotroph > necrotroph for PTI/ETI studies); (iii) availability of genetic tools and resources; (iv) speed of infection cycle and ease of artificial inoculation; (v) existing virulence diversity; and (vi) agricultural relevance.\n\n#### Table 1. Comparative Assessment of Top Candidate Pathogens\n\n| Criterion | *Peronospora variabilis* | *P. syringae* pv. *aptata* | *P. syringae* pv. *tomato* DC3000 | *Botrytis cinerea* |\n|-----------|--------------------------|----------------------------|-----------------------------------|---------------------|\n| **Confirmed on *C. pallidicaule*** | ✅ Yes (Rollano-Peñaloza et al., 2021) | ❌ Not directly; on *C. quinoa* | ❌ No | ❌ Not specifically reported |\n| **Lifestyle** | Obligate biotroph | Hemibiotroph | Hemibiotroph | Necrotroph |\n| **Immunity relevance** | PTI/ETI, SA pathway, HR, gene-for-gene | PTI/ETI, SA/JA pathways, T3SS effectors | PTI/ETI, SA/JA pathways, gold-standard T3E toolkit | JA/ET pathway, necrotroph counter-defenses |\n| **Genetic tools** | ⚠️ Developing (transcriptomics, COX2/ITS markers) | Growing (2 genomes: P16, P21; T3E repertoire) | **Excellent** (complete genome; 36 T3Es; transposon libraries; CRISPR) | Good (genome sequenced; mutants available) |\n| **Infection cycle** | 9–11 days to sporulation | 3–7 days to visible symptoms | 3–5 days | 5–10 days |\n| **Inoculation ease** | Spray + 24 h humidity | Spray or infiltrate; axenic culture | Spray or infiltrate; axenic culture | Wound or aerosol; easy |\n| **Virulence diversity** | 4 virulence groups (V1–V4); 3 R-factors | Multiple strains with different virulence (P16 vs. P21) | Many mutants; effectorless D36E polymutant available | Broad genetic diversity but less structured |\n| **Maintainability** | Requires living host (quinoa) every 2 weeks | Easy: LB agar, −80°C glycerol stocks | Easy: same as above | Easy: mycelial storage; sclerotia |\n\n### 3.2 Primary Recommendation: *Peronospora variabilis*\n\n**Justification — six pillars:**\n\n**(a) Confirmed natural compatibility.** *P. variabilis* is the only pathogen formally documented to cause disease on *C. pallidicaule* in its native range. Rollano-Peñaloza et al. (2021) isolated the pathogen from symptomatic plants in Bolivia, fulfilled Koch's postulates through artificial re-inoculation onto three cañahua varieties, and confirmed identity by PCR and Sanger sequencing of PvCox2 (99.8% identity to quinoa isolate) and PvITS (100% identity). This eliminates the need for pathogen discovery or host-range adaptation—the most time-consuming barrier in pathosystem establishment.\n\n**(b) Obligate biotroph—ideal for plant immunity studies.** As an obligate biotroph, *P. variabilis* must maintain living host cells, deploying haustoria to extract nutrients while suppressing host defenses. This forces the plant to mount sustained PTI and ETI responses, making the system analogous to the world-class model *Arabidopsis*–*H. arabidopsidis*. Biotrophs predominantly activate salicylic acid (SA)-dependent defense pathways and are the classic system for studying gene-for-gene resistance (R gene–Avr gene recognition) (Kamoun et al., 2015).\n\n**(c) Established virulence diversity.** Ochoa et al. (1999) identified **four virulence groups (V1–V4)** among 20 Ecuatorian *P. variabilis* isolates tested on 60 quinoa accessions, corresponding to at least three postulated resistance factors (R1, R2, R3). V4 is the most virulent, overcoming all known resistance factors. This diversity allows simultaneous study of both compatible (disease) and incompatible (resistance/HR) interactions within a single pathogen species.\n\n**(d) Rapid and reproducible infection cycle.** Under greenhouse conditions (17–25°C, high humidity), chlorotic lesions appear at 7–9 days post-inoculation (dpi), abundant sporulation occurs by 11 dpi, and new urediniospores can re-infect within 7–9 days. This enables multiple infection cycles per month and rapid iteration of experiments.\n\n**(e) Existing differential host set and reference cultivars.** A differential set of quinoa lines (ECU-288 [susceptible check], ECU-291 [R1], ECU-270 [R2], ECU-379 [R3]) was established by Ochoa et al. (1999), and additional reference cultivars (Puno, Titicaca, Vikinga, Real, Kurmi) with characterized susceptibility ratings exist (Colque-Little et al., 2021). This framework can be directly adapted for *C. pallidicaule*.\n\n**(f) Agricultural relevance.** Downy mildew causes yield losses of 30–50% in tolerant quinoa cultivars and near-total loss in susceptible ones (Colque-Little et al., 2021). Identifying and understanding resistance in *C. pallidicaule* would directly benefit quinoa and cañahua production in the Andes and beyond.\n\n### 3.3 Secondary/Complementary Recommendation: *Pseudomonas syringae* pv. *aptata*\n\nFor molecular dissection requiring superior genetic manipulability, I recommend establishing a parallel bacterial pathosystem with *P. syringae* pv. *aptata* (strain P21). This bacterium:\n\n- Naturally infects beet, Swiss chard, and spinach—all Amaranthaceae, phylogenetically proximal to *C. pallidicaule*.\n- Has two fully sequenced genomes (strains P16 and P21; Ranković et al., 2023) with characterized T3SS effector repertoires (15–25 effectors including AvrRpm1, HopAW1, HopAU1, HopM1, AvrE1).\n- Can be grown axenically on LB agar, stored at −80°C as glycerol stocks, and manipulated via conjugation, transposon mutagenesis, and CRISPR-Cas9.\n- Produces visible water-soaked necrotic lesions within 3–5 days of infiltration.\n- The effectorless D36E polymutant approach (Mendel et al., 2025) demonstrated in spinach provides a platform for heterologous effector functional analysis.\n\n**Caveat:** *P. syringae* pv. *aptata* has not yet been formally reported on *C. pallidicaule* (only on *C. quinoa*; Fonseca-Guerra et al., 2021). Its establishment therefore constitutes a **Phase II objective**, to be pursued in parallel with but contingent upon the operational status of the primary *P. variabilis* pathosystem.\n\n---\n\n## 4. TERMINOLOGY: \"PATHOVAR\" IN THE CONTEXT OF *PERONOSPORA VARIABILIS*\n\nIt is important to clarify nomenclature. In bacteria, **pathovar** (pv.) is a formal infraspecific rank defined by the International Code of Nomenclature of Prokaryotes, based on host specificity. Oomycetes do not use the pathovar concept. Instead, host-specificity within *P. variabilis* is described using:\n\n- **Virulence groups (VG) or races**: Defined by differential infection patterns on a set of host differential genotypes (Ochoa et al., 1999). Four groups are recognized: V1 (least virulent, resisted by R1), V2 (overcomes R1, resisted by R2), V3 (overcomes R1–R2, resisted by R3), and V4 (overcomes R1–R3, most aggressive).\n- **Formae speciales (f.sp.)**: Historically *P. variabilis* was treated as *P. farinosa* f.sp. *chenopodii*, but molecular phylogenetics established it as a distinct species (Choi et al., 2015).\n- **Isolate designations**: By geographic origin, host species, and collector (e.g., \"Kari\" isolate from Bolivia).\n\nThroughout this report, I use **\"pathovar\" informally** to mean a **distinct virulence class (race/virulence group) within *P. variabilis***, and **\"pathovar\" for bacteria** in the formal sense when discussing *P. syringae*.\n\n---\n\n## 5. RAPID VIRULENCE SCREENING PROTOCOL\n\nI propose a **three-tiered screening pipeline** designed to rapidly rank isolate virulence on *C. pallidicaule* while simultaneously scoring the susceptibility of diverse host accessions.\n\n```\nTier 1: Quarantine & Isolation\n    ↓\nTier 2: Leaf-Disk Dose-Response Microassay (High-Throughput)\n    ↓\nTier 3: Full-Plant Greenhouse Confirmation Assay\n```\n\n### 5.1 Tier 1: Pathogen Acquisition, Isolation, and Spore Production\n\n**Step 1.1 — Acquisition of isolates.** Obtain *P. variabilis* isolates from:\n- Quinoa research stations in Bolivia (PROINPA, Cochabamba Valley) and Peru (UNALM, Madre de Dios).\n- The Ochoa et al. (1999) collection of 20 Ecuatorian isolates (via collaboration).\n- International collections: Spain (IRIAF, Madrid—Fondevilla et al., 2023), USA (USDA-ARS, NH; ANSUC collection—Testen et al., 2014), Egypt, India, Korea.\n- Include isolates from both quinoa and *C. album* (common lambsquarters, a known alternate host).\n\n**Step 1.2 — Single-spore isolation and purification.**\n1. Collect heavily sporulating leaves from infected quinoa cv. 'Real' (highly susceptible universal host).\n2. Under a stereo microscope, transfer individual sporangia from sporangiophores into separate 1-well trays containing two 4-week-old quinoa cv. 'Real' seedlings using a fine glass capillary.\n3. Grow isolated plants individually in greenhouse compartments (17–25°C, 12-h photoperiod) to confirm clean infection.\n4. Transfer purified isolates to cryovials (sporangia in water + 10% DMSO) and store at −80°C, or maintain by biweekly passage on quinoa cv. 'Real'.\n\n**Step 1.3 — Spore production for screening.**\n1. At 9–12 dpi, gently brush sporangia from abaxial leaf surfaces into sterile distilled water containing 0.01% Tween 20 and 25 µg/mL propiconazole (to suppress contaminating fungi).\n2. Filter through double-layer cheesecloth.\n3. Count spores using a Neubauer hemocytometer.\n4. Adjust concentration to **1 × 10⁶ spores/mL** for standard inoculation.\n5. Verify viability: stain aliquot with I₂/KI; ≥80% viable spores required.\n\n### 5.2 Tier 2: Leaf-Disk Dose-Response Microassay\n\n**Purpose:** High-throughput ranking of isolate virulence and host susceptibility in a space-efficient, rapid format.\n\n**Method:**\n\n1. **Plant preparation:** Sow surface-sterilized *C. pallidicaule* seeds in plug trays (peat:perlite 1:1), stratify at 4°C for 48 h, then germinate at 22°C under 16-h light. Use 4-week-old seedlings at the 3–4 true-leaf stage.\n\n2. **Leaf disk preparation:** Punch 8-mm diameter leaf disks from fully expanded true leaves using a cork borer, avoiding major veins. Handle with fine forceps to avoid tissue damage.\n\n3. **Inoculation:** Place disks abaxial-side up on 50-µL droplets of spore suspension in 24-well plates (1 disk/well). Include control treatments (sterile water + Tween 20 + propiconazole). For dose-response, prepare serial dilutions: 10³, 10⁴, 10⁵, 10⁶, 10⁷ spores/mL.\n\n4. **Wet period:** After inoculation, incubate plates in darkness at 22°C for 24 h to promote sporangial germination and penetration (≥95% RH achievable by covering plates with sealed lids).\n\n5. **Dry period:** Transfer disks to moistened filter paper in sealed plastic containers and incubate under 12-h UV-fluorescent light at 20–22°C.\n\n6. **Scoring timeline:** Score at 5, 7, 9, and 12 dpi.\n\n7. **Disease severity scale (adapted from Ochoa et al., 1999; Colque-Little et al., 2021):**\n\n| Score | Description | % Severity Equivalent | Sporulation |\n|-------|-------------|----------------------|-------------|\n| 0 | Immune; no symptoms | 0% | None |\n| 1 | Small chlorotic spots (<2 mm), localized | 1–10% | None |\n| 2 | Chlorotic spots (2–5 mm), limited sporulation | 10–25% | Light on abaxial surface |\n| 3 | Large chlorotic/necrotic lesions (>5 mm), moderate sporulation | 25–50% | Abundant on abaxial surface |\n| 4 | Extensive necrosis, wilting, heavy sporulation | 50–75% | Both adaxial and abaxial |\n| 5 | Whole-leaf necrosis, plant collapse | 75–100% | Profuse |\n\n8. **Quantitative metrics:** For each isolate × accession combination, calculate:\n   - **Mean disease severity** at peak (9–12 dpi)\n   - **Area Under the Disease Severity Track (AUDST)** \n   - **Sporulation index**: ratio of sporulation coverage to disease severity (Colque-Little et al., 2021)\n   - **EC₅₀** from dose-response curves (non-linear regression, 4-parameter logistic model)\n\n**Throughput:** A single 24-well plate accommodates 24 isolate × accession combinations. With 10 isolates × 20 accessions = 200 treatments, 3 plates with replicates suffice for an initial screen (~2–3 days of hands-on work). This enables completion of the primary screening phase within **3–4 weeks**.\n\n### 5.3 Tier 3: Full-Plant Greenhouse Confirmation Assay\n\n**Purpose:** Validate Tier 2 findings under realistic growth conditions with whole plants.\n\n**Method:**\n\n1. Sow *C. pallidicaule* seeds in 10-cm pots (sterile pasteurized soil mix: peat:vermiculite:perlite 2:1:1). Grow in greenhouse at 22 ± 2°C, 12-h photoperiod.\n\n2. At the 3–4 true-leaf stage (~3 weeks old), select uniform seedlings for inoculation.\n\n3. **Spray inoculation:** Immerse entire plant upside-down into spore suspension (1 × 10⁶ spores/mL) for 30 s, then spray to runoff with atomizer. Ensure thorough coverage of abaxial leaf surfaces where stomata (the primary infection sites) are located.\n\n4. **Humidity treatment:** Immediately cover plants with transparent polyethylene bags to maintain ≥95% RH. Maintain covers for 24 h.\n\n5. **Incubation:** Remove bags and return to greenhouse at 17–25°C under natural light (12-h photoperiod). Soil moisture maintained at field capacity.\n\n6. **Scoring:** Assess disease severity at 5, 7, 9, 11, and 14 dpi using the same 0–5 scale. Record:\n   - **Disease incidence** (% plants showing any symptoms)\n   - **Mean severity** across plants\n   - **Area Under the Disease Progression Curve (AUDPC)**\n   - **Sporulation** (% leaf area sporulating)\n\n7. **Statistical design:** Randomized complete block design (RCBD) with 4–6 replicates per combination. Include positive controls (quinoa cv. 'Real' inoculated with same isolate) and negative controls (mock-inoculated *C. pallidicaule*).\n\n8. **Selected isolate × accession combinations from Tier 2:** Advance the top 5 most virulent isolates and the top 10 most susceptible and most resistant *C. pallidicaule* accessions.\n\n### 5.4 Environmental Conditioning Optimization\n\nConduct a factorial experiment (temperature × humidity × light × growth stage) to identify conditions maximizing disease consistency:\n\n| Factor | Levels Tested |\n|--------|---------------|\n| Night temperature | 10, 15, 17, 20, 25°C |\n| Day temperature | 20, 25, 30°C |\n| Humidity duration | 12, 18, 24, 36 h |\n| Post-inoculation light | Darkness, 12 h, 24 h continuous |\n| Growth stage | Seedling (3 wk), juvenile (5 wk), mature (8 wk) |\n\nBased on quinoa data, the optimum is expected to be **17°C night temperature with 24 h high humidity** (Colque-Little et al., 2021; Rollano-Peñaloza et al., 2022).\n\n### 5.5 Bacterial Pathosystem Screening (Phase II)\n\nFor *P. syringae* pv. *aptata*:\n\n1. Grow bacteria on King's B agar at 28°C for 48 h.\n2. Harvest and resuspend in sterile water + 0.02% Silwet L-77 to OD₆₀₀ = 0.2 (~1 × 10⁸ CFU/mL).\n3. Prepare serial dilutions: 10⁶, 10⁷, 10⁸ CFU/mL.\n4. **Syringe infiltration:** Inflate abaxial leaf intercellular space with 10 µL of suspension using a blunt 22-gauge needle (no syringe needle). Mark infiltrated spots with waterproof pen.\n5. **Spray inoculation:** Spray to runoff as for *P. variabilis*.\n6. Score at 2, 3, 5, and 7 dpi: water-soaked lesions, chlorosis, necrosis, HR.\n7. Quantify bacterial growth: excise leaf discs, surface-sterilize (70% ethanol, 1 min), homogenize in sterile water, serial dilute, plate on LB + CFC selective medium. Count CFU at 48 h.\n\n---\n\n## 6. DETERMINATION OF THE MOST SUITABLE PATHOVAR\n\n### 6.1 Differential Host Set for Virulence Profiling\n\nAdapting the quinoa differential set (Ochoa et al., 1999) for *C. pallidicaule*:\n\n| Designation | Genotype | Postulated R-genes | Virulence Groups Overcome | Role |\n|-------------|----------|---------------------|---------------------------|------|\n| **S** | *C. pallidicaule* cv. 'Bol 1.1' or most susceptible accession | None (or unknown) | All | Susceptible check |\n| **D1** | Quinoa line ECU-291 | R1 | V1 | Differentiates V1 from V2–V4 |\n| **D2** | Quinoa line ECU-270 | R2 | V1, V2 | Differentiates V2 from V3–V4 |\n| **D3** | Quinoa line ECU-379 | R3 | V1, V2, V3 | Differentiates V3 from V4 |\n| **D4** | Quinoa line with R4 or *C. pallidicaule* accession showing HR to V4 | R4 | V1–V4 | Detects V4 |\n| **SU** | *C. pallidicaule* accession showing strongest HR | Unknown | Unknown | Candidate for novel R gene |\n\nAdditionally, include *C. album* (common lambsquarters) as a universal susceptible check, since *P. variabilis* isolates from quinoa and *C. album* cross-infect each other (Colque-Little et al., 2021; Nolen et al., 2022).\n\n### 6.2 Cross-Inoculation Protocol for Pathovar Determination\n\n**Phase A: Assembly.**\n1. Assemble 10–20 *P. variabilis* isolates representing geographic and host diversity.\n2. Molecularly characterize each isolate via ITS and COX2 sequencing (Testen et al., 2014; Fondevilla et al., 2023).\n\n**Phase B: Differential inoculation.**\n1. Inoculate each isolate on:\n   - The differential quinoa set (D1–D4, S)\n   - 20–30 *C. pallidicaule* accessions (from germplasm collections)\n   - *C. album* (universal susceptible check)\n   - *C. quinoa* cv. 'Real' (positive control) and cv. 'Kurmi' (tolerant reference)\n2. Use the standardized spray + 24 h humidity protocol.\n3. Score at 9–12 dpi using the 0–5 scale.\n\n**Phase C: Classification.**\nClassify each isolate into a virulence group based on its reaction pattern on the differential set:\n\n| Virulence Group | Infects | Excluded by | R-genes overcome |\n|-----------------|---------|-------------|------------------|\n| **V1** | S, D2, D3, D4 | D1 | None |\n| **V2** | S, D3, D4 | D1, D2 | R1 |\n| **V3** | S, D4 | D1, D2, D3 | R1, R2 |\n| **V4** | S, D1, D2, D3, D4 | — | R1, R2, R3 |\n| **Novel type** | Unexpected patterns | — | Candidate for new race/pathovar designation |\n\nIf *C. pallidicaule* accessions show differential resistance patterns distinct from quinoa, this may reveal new virulence groups or R-gene specificities not previously documented.\n\n### 6.3 Molecular Characterization of Pathovars\n\n1. **DNA barcoding:** Sequence ITS (Internal Transcribed Spacer) and COX2 (Cytochrome c Oxidase Subunit 2) regions for all isolates. Construct a maximum-likelihood phylogenetic tree. Fondevilla et al. (2023) demonstrated that *P. variabilis* isolates cluster primarily by geographic location rather than host species—this should be verified for *C. pallidicaule*-associated isolates.\n\n2. **Effector profiling:** If RxLR effector genes are available for *P. variabilis* (or related species such as *P. effusa*), perform PCR-based screening for presence/absence of known effector alleles across isolates. Alternatively, conduct RNA-seq of the pathogen transcriptome during infection of susceptible vs. resistant *C. pallidicaule* tissues to identify differentially expressed effector candidates.\n\n3. **Correlation of molecular and virulence data:** Test whether virulence groups correspond to monophyletic clades (indicating a genetic basis for pathovar classification) or are paraphyletic (indicating that virulence is determined by horizontally acquired elements such as effector genes on transposable elements).\n\n### 6.4 Criteria for Selecting the Best Pathovar(s)\n\n| Criterion | Weight | Rationale |\n|-----------|--------|-----------|\n| Strong virulence on susceptible *C. pallidicaule* genotype | **High** | Required for studying disease processes; needs robust, scorable phenotype |\n| Induction of HR on resistant *C. pallidicaule* accessions | **High** | Required for studying resistance/ETI mechanisms |\n| Genetic stability (consistent virence across passages) | Medium | Ensures reproducibility across experiments and over time |\n| Representativeness (matches dominant field races) | Medium | Ensures agricultural relevance of findings |\n| High sporulation capacity | Medium | Facilitates large-scale inoculum production |\n| Distinct molecular signature | Low | Enables tracking, communication, and deposition in culture collections |\n\n---\n\n## 7. LOGICAL EXPERIMENTAL STEPS AND EXPECTED OUTCOMES\n\n### 7.1 Layered Reasoning Chain (R1–R13)\n\nThe following numbered nodes form the explicit evidential chain from low-level observations to final conclusions. Each node includes: (a) the claim, (b) the evidence/derivation, and (c) dependencies.\n\n---\n\n**R1 — *C. pallidicaule* is a member of the Amaranthaceae family, subfamily Chenopodioideae, closely related to quinoa (*C. quinoa*), spinach (*S. oleracea*), and beet (*B. vulgaris*).**\n- (a) Claim: Taxonomic placement of *C. pallidicaule*.\n- (b) Evidence: Mangelson et al. (2019) genome assembly and phylogenomic analysis placing *C. pallidicaule* as diploid ancestor/proxy for the A-subgenome of allotetraploid quinoa; strong synteny confirmed.\n- (c) Dependencies: None (foundational taxonomic fact).\n\n**R2 — *Peronospora variabilis* is a natural obligate biotrophic pathogen of *Chenopodium* species, including *C. pallidicaule*.**\n- (a) Claim: *P. variabilis* naturally infects *C. pallidicaule*.\n- (b) Evidence: Rollano-Peñaloza et al. (2021) collected sporulating leaves from symptomatic *C. pallidicaule* plants in Bolivia; the pathogen was re-isolated via artificial inoculation onto three cañahua varieties; identity confirmed by PvCox2 (99.8% identity) and PvITS (100% identity) Sanger sequencing. Earlier reports suggested resistance (Alandia et al., 1979), but the 2021 study provides definitive molecular confirmation of susceptibility.\n- (c) Dependencies: R1 (host taxonomy determines pathogen host-range context).\n\n**R3 — *P. variabilis* has an established virulence classification with four groups (V1–V4) and corresponding resistance factors (R1–R3) in quinoa.**\n- (a) Claim: Virulence diversity exists and is classified.\n- (b) Evidence: Ochoa et al. (1999) tested 20 Ecuadorian isolates on 60 quinoa accessions and postulated four virulence groups based on differential infection patterns on four quinoa lines (ECU-288, ECU-291, ECU-270, ECU-379). Colque-Little et al. (2021) confirmed significant genetic variation for disease severity (5–83%) and sporulation (0.2–83.6%) across 132 quinoa genotypes, validating the qualitative resistance framework.\n- (c) Dependencies: R2 (the pathogen exists and infects Chenopodium).\n\n**R4 — The obligate biotrophic lifestyle of *P. variabilis* makes it an ideal model for studying PTI and ETI, the two tiers of the plant immune system.**\n- (a) Claim: Biotrophs are optimal for immunity research.\n- (b) Evidence: Obligate biotrophs require living host tissue and secrete effector proteins (RxLR and Crinkler classes) into host cells to suppress PTI (Kamoun et al., 2015; Baxter et al., 2010). When recognized by corresponding NLR resistance proteins, these effectors trigger ETI and HR. This gene-for-gene architecture is the classical paradigm of plant pathology (Flor, 1971) and has been most thoroughly elucidated in the *Arabidopsis*–*H. arabidopsidis* system.\n- (c) Dependencies: R2 (pathogen lifestyle).\n\n**R5 — The 9–11 day infection cycle of *P. variabilis* under optimized greenhouse conditions enables rapid phenotyping.**\n- (a) Claim: Fast life cycle.\n- (b) Evidence: Rollano-Peñaloza et al. (2021) observed chlorotic lesions at 9 dpi and abundant sporulation at 11 dpi after spray inoculation of *C. pallidicaule* with *P. variabilis* sporangia at 17–25°C under high humidity.\n- (c) Dependencies: R2.\n\n**R6 — A leaf-disk assay can enable high-throughput, quantitative screening of *P. variabilis* isolate virulence on *C. pallidicaule*.**\n- (a) Claim: Leaf-disk assay is feasible and quantitative.\n- (b) Evidence: Leaf-disk assays are standard for many foliar pathogens. For *P. variabilis*, floating abaxial-side-up leaf disks on spore suspensions followed by 24 h humidity and 12-h light produces consistent infection (adapted from protocols for *H. arabidopsidis* on *Arabidopsis*; Bio-Protocol 1627). Disease severity scoring on a 0–5 scale and AUDST calculation provide quantitative metrics. Dose-response curves (10³–10⁷ spores/mL) yield EC₅₀ values for virulence comparison.\n- (c) Dependencies: R2, R5.\n\n**R7 — Screening a panel of 10–20 *P. variabilis* isolates on 20–30 *C. pallidicaule* accessions using the leaf-disk assay will identify the most virulent isolates and the most susceptible/resistant host accessions within 3–4 weeks.**\n- (a) Claim: Screening is rapid and informative.\n- (b) Evidence: Throughput calculation: 24-well plate accommodates 24 treatments; 10 isolates × 20 accessions = 200 treatments, requiring ~3 plates with replicates. Hands-on work: ~2–3 days. Incubation and scoring: 9–12 days. Data analysis: ~1 day. Total: ~3 weeks from start to virulence ranking.\n- (c) Dependencies: R6.\n\n**R8 — Cross-inoculation of *P. variabilis* isolates on a differential host set (quinoa lines + *C. pallidicaule* accessions) will classify isolates into virulence groups and may reveal *C. pallidicaule*-specific virulence types.**\n- (a) Claim: Differential host set enables pathovar determination.\n- (b) Evidence: The quinoa differential set (ECU-288, ECU-291, ECU-270, ECU-379) has been validated by Ochoa et al. (1999) and Colque-Little et al. (2021). Extension to include *C. pallidicaule* accessions (especially cv. 'Bol 1.1', which shows HR-like lesions; Rollano-Peñaloza et al., 2021) will test whether the resistance specificity is conserved across Chenopodium species. If *C. pallidicaule* isolates show virulence patterns not matching V1–V4, they may represent novel virulence groups.\n- (c) Dependencies: R3, R2.\n\n**R9 — Virulence Group 4 (V4) isolates are predicted to be the most suitable pathovars for studying disease progression and susceptibility mechanisms because they overcome R1–R3 and produce robust compatible interactions on the widest range of genotypes.**\n- (a) Claim: V4 is best for disease studies.\n- (b) Evidence: V4 overcomes all known resistance factors (Ochoa et al., 1999), is the most virulent group, has been detected on multiple continents (Spain, USA, Ecuador; Fondevilla et al., 2023), and is predicted to infect *C. pallidicaule* aggressively. A strongly compatible interaction ensures scorable, quantifiable disease for physiological, biochemical, and molecular studies.\n- (c) Dependencies: R3, R8.\n\n**R10 — V1 or V2 isolates are predicted to be the most suitable for studying resistance mechanisms, provided a resistant *C. pallidicaule* accession exists that carries a functional R1 (or equivalent) gene.**\n- (a) Claim: Less virulent isolates are needed for resistance studies.\n- (b) Evidence: V1 is the least virulent group, resisted by R1. cv. 'Bol 1.1' of *C. pallidicaule* shows HR-like lesions upon *P. variabilis* infection (Rollano-Peñaloza et al., 2021), suggesting it may carry a functional R1 ortholog. If V1 cannot overcome this resistance, the interaction will display classical gene-for-gene HR—ideal for dissecting ETI signaling.\n- (c) Dependencies: R3, R8.\n\n**R11 — *Pseudomonas syringae* pv. *aptata* (strain P21) is a suitable complementary bacterial pathogen for molecular studies, given its Amaranthaceae host range, sequenced genome, and characterized T3SS effector repertoire.**\n- (a) Claim: pv. *aptata* is a good secondary model.\n- (b) Evidence: pv. *aptata* naturally infects beet and spinach (Amaranthaceae); strain P21 is highly virulent with a broad host range within the family (Ranković et al., 2023). It shares T3SS effectors (HopM1, AvrE1) with the model strain DC3000, enabling cross-referencing of molecular tools. The hemibiotrophic lifestyle engages both SA and JA/ET pathways, complementing the SA-dominated biotroph response.\n- (c) Dependencies: R1 (host phylogeny informs pathogen host-range probability).\n\n**R12 — A four-phase experimental plan (pathosystem establishment → virulence/host-range screening → pathovar determination → molecular dissection) will take 26 weeks to establish a validated, reproducible pathosystem, and 3 years for full molecular characterization.**\n- (a) Claim: Timeline is realistic and comprehensive.\n- (b) Evidence: Phase I (weeks 1–4): pathogen acquisition, isolation, and initial compatibility confirmation. Phase II (weeks 5–12): Tier 2 leaf-disk screening and Tier 3 full-plant confirmation. Phase III (weeks 13–26): differential host profiling, molecular characterization, and pathovar designation. Phase IV (months 6–36): transcriptomics, effector discovery, resistance gene mapping, and functional validation. These timelines are derived from published quinoa downy mildew studies (Colque-Little et al., 2021; Rollano-Peñaloza et al., 2022) and standard plant pathology workflows.\n- (c) Dependencies: R5, R7, R8, R9, R10.\n\n**R13 — The validated pathosystem will enable genetic mapping of resistance genes in *C. pallidicaule*, identification of pathogen avirulence (Avr) genes, and ultimately transfer of resistance to quinoa.**\n- (a) Claim: Long-term impact.\n- (b) Evidence: The *C. pallidicaule* diploid genome is sequenced and genetically tractable (Mangelson et al., 2019). Mapping populations (F₂, RILs) derived from resistant × susceptible crosses can be phenotyped for downy mildew resistance using the validated pathosystem. QTL mapping and candidate gene cloning are feasible, drawing on established methods from quinoa (Colque-Little et al., 2021). Resistance genes identified in *C. pallidicaule* can be bridged to quinoa through hybridization (C. pallidicaule × C. quinoa) or gene editing.\n- (c) Dependencies: R9, R10, R12.\n\n---\n\n### 7.2 Detailed Experimental Work Plan\n\n#### Phase I: Pathosystem Establishment (Weeks 1–4)\n\n| Step | Action | Resources Needed | Expected Outcome |\n|------|--------|-----------------|------------------|\n| I.1 | Collect/obtain *C. pallidicaule* germplasm (minimum 50 accessions from Andean genebanks: SANIPED, PROINPA, UNALM; and local landraces) | Greenhouse space, collaboration agreements | Established germplasm collection |\n| I.2 | Obtain *P. variabilis* isolates (10–20 isolates from Bolivia, Ecuador, Spain, USA) | Phytosanitary permits, collaboration with Rollano-Peñaloza et al. (2021) and Fondevilla et al. (2023) | Initial isolate library |\n| I.3 | Single-spore isolation; maintain purified isolates on quinoa cv. 'Real' | Stereo microscope, glass capillaries, growth cabinets | Pure, identifiable isolates |\n| I.4 | Optimize inoculation protocol: test spore concentrations (10⁴–10⁷/mL), humidity durations (12–36 h), temperatures (15–25°C) on 10 *C. pallidicaule* accessions | Standard greenhouse setup | SOP for optimal inoculation conditions |\n| I.5 | Confirm pathogenicity on *C. pallidicaule* following Koch's postulates | Molecular identification reagents | Published confirmation (if not already) |\n\n#### Phase II: Virulence and Host Range Screening (Weeks 5–12)\n\n| Step | Action | Expected Outcome |\n|------|--------|-----------------|\n| II.1 | Tier 2 leaf-disk assay: 10–20 isolates × 20–30 *C. pallidicaule* accessions + dose-response curves | Virulence ranking of isolates; susceptibility classification of accessions; EC₅₀ values |\n| II.2 | Identify \"hot\" isolates (highest virulence on *C. pallidicaule*) and \"resistant\" accessions (HR or low severity) | Candidate isolates for Phase III; candidate resistance sources |\n| II.3 | Tier 3 full-plant assay: top 5 isolates × top 10 accessions (most susceptible + most resistant) | Confirmatory data; AUDPS values; detailed disease phenology; sporulation quantification |\n| II.4 | Reproducibility trial: repeat core experiment with different operator | CV < 20% for disease severity |\n\n#### Phase III: Pathovar Determination (Weeks 8–18)\n\n| Step | Action | Expected Outcome |\n|------|--------|-----------------|\n| III.1 | Assemble differential quinoa set (ECU-288, ECU-291, ECU-270, ECU-379) + *C. pallidicaule* accessions showing distinct reactions | Differential set established in greenhouse |\n| III.2 | Cross-inoculation matrix: all isolates × differential set | Virulence profile for each isolate |\n| III.3 | Classify isolates into VG1–VG4; identify novel virulence types | First pathovar catalog for *P. variabilis* on *C. pallidicaule* |\n| III.4 | Molecular barcoding (ITS + COX2) of all isolates; construct phylogenetic tree | Correlation of molecular data with virulence profiles |\n| III.5 | Designate reference pathovar strains (one per VG) deposited in culture collection (e.g., CFBP, USDA-ARS) | Permanent reference collection |\n\n#### Phase IV: Molecular Dissection of Immunity (Months 6–36)\n\n| Step | Action | Expected Outcome |\n|------|--------|-----------------|\n| IV.1 | Time-course RNA-seq of compatible (V4 × susceptible) and incompatible (V1 × resistant) interactions at 0, 6, 12, 24, 48, 72 hpi | Transcriptome dynamics; differentially expressed host and pathogen genes |\n| IV.2 | Identify RxLR effector candidates from *P. variabilis* expressed in *C. pallidicaule* | Candidate Avr genes |\n| IV.3 | Generate mapping population (F₂ or RILs from resistant × susceptible *C. pallidicaule* cross) | Segregating population for QTL mapping |\n| IV.4 | Phenotype mapping population for disease severity with selected pathovar; GBS for genotyping | QTL identification for resistance |\n| IV.5 | Functional validation via transient overexpression, VIGS, or stable transformation in *C. pallidicaule* | Confirmation of R gene function |\n| IV.6 | Compare with quinoa orthologs to understand evolutionary dynamics of immunity in Chenopodium | Insights into arms race evolution |\n\n---\n\n## 8. STATISTICAL FRAMEWORK\n\n### 8.1 Experimental Design\n\n- **Tier 2 (leaf-disk):** Completely randomized design with factorial arrangement (isolate × accession). Minimum 3 biological replicates per combination.\n- **Tier 3 (full-plant):** Randomized complete block design (RCBD) with 4–6 replicates. Block = growth chamber run or potting batch.\n- **Differential host profiling:** RCBD with 3 replicates per isolate × differential genotype combination.\n\n### 8.2 Data Analysis\n\n**Continuous data (disease severity %, log CFU, chlorophyll content):**\n- One-way ANOVA for comparing virulence among pathovars/isolates.\n- Two-way ANOVA for accession × isolate interactions.\n- If normality/homoscedasticity assumptions violated: Kruskal-Wallis H-test with Dunn's post-hoc.\n- Post-hoc pairwise comparisons: Tukey's HSD.\n\n**Ordinal data (disease scores 0–5):**\n- Proportional odds logistic regression (cumulative link model) or Jonckheere-Terpstra test for ordered alternatives.\n\n**Dose-response curves:**\n- Non-linear four-parameter logistic regression: $y = d + \\frac{a - d}{1 + \\exp(b(x - c))}$ where $a$ = lower asymptote, $d$ = upper asymptote, $b$ = slope, $c$ = EC₅₀.\n- Compare EC₅₀ values between pathovars using extra sum-of-squares F-test.\n\n**Heritability estimation (broad-sense):**\n$$H^2 = \\frac{\\sigma^2_G}{\\sigma^2_G + \\sigma^2_{G\\times E}/e + \\sigma^2_E/(e \\times r)}$$\n\nwhere $\\sigma^2_G$ = genetic variance, $\\sigma^2_{G\\times E}$ = genotype × environment variance, $\\sigma^2_E$ = error variance, $e$ = number of environments, $r$ = number of replicates (Falconer & Mackay, 1996).\n\n### 8.3 Sample Size Justification\n\nBased on power calculation ($\\alpha = 0.05$, $1-\\beta = 0.80$, effect size $d = 1.33$): **≥9 independent biological replicates per group** for pairwise comparisons. For multi-pathovar ANOVA with 5 groups: **≥10 replicates per pathovar**.\n\n---\n\n## 9. UNCERTAINTIES, RISKS, AND MITIGATION STRATEGIES\n\n| # | Uncertainty / Risk | Impact | Mitigation |\n|---|-------------------|--------|------------|\n| 1 | *P. variabilis* may not sporulate abundantly on *C. pallidicaule* under the researcher's specific conditions | Low sporulation limits inoculum supply for high-throughput screening | Optimize humidity, temperature, and nutrient conditions; maintain pathogen on quinoa cv. 'Real' and periodically challenge *C. pallidicaule*; use detached leaf assay for sporulation boost |\n| 2 | *C. pallidicaule* may be universally resistant to all *P. variabilis* isolates, precluding disease process studies | Cannot study compatible interaction or susceptibility mechanisms | Screen wild *Chenopodium* relatives (*C. berlandieri*, *C. ficifolium*) for susceptibility; if all Chenopodium species are resistant, pivot to *P. syringae* pv. *aptata* as primary system |\n| 3 | The quinoa differential set (R1–R3) may not correspond to equivalent resistance specificities in *C. pallidicaule* | Pathovar classification may not translate | Empirically determine virulence groups on *C. pallidicaule* using the differential set as a starting point; construct a new statistical differential set from *C. pallidicaule* accessions showing distinct resistance spectra |\n| 4 | *P. syringae* pv. *aptata* may fail to infect *C. pallidicaule* | Bacterial secondary pathosystem fails | Fall back to *P. syringae* pv. *tomato* DC3000, which has been shown to survive in spinach leaves (Mendel et al., 2025); use wound inoculation to overcome non-host resistance; employ *Nicotiana benthamiana* as surrogate host for initial characterization |\n| 5 | Genetic transformation of *C. pallidicaule* may be recalcitrant | Limits functional validation of candidate genes | Use VIGS (virus-induced gene silencing) based on *Nicotiana benthamiana* efi-a-induced silencing vector (pTRV) adapted to *C. pallidicaule*; employ transient expression in *N. benthamiana* as proxy; use *C. pallidicaule* protoplasts for subcellular localization and VIGS |\n| 6 | Pathogen genetic stability may degrade during prolonged maintenance on quinoa | Loss of virulence or change in pathovar identity | Minimize passages; create DNA and spore stocks at −80°C; regularly re-confirm virulence profile against differential set |\n| 7 | Field emergence of *P. variabilis* in *C. pallidicaule* may differ from greenhouse observations | Greenhouse-validated pathosystem may not reflect field complexity | Include field trials in Andean region (Bolivia/Peru) in Year 2; monitor natural infection pressure; test pathogen fitness under field conditions |\n\n---\n\n## 10. ALTERNATIVE SCENARIOS AND CONTINGENCY PLANS\n\n### Scenario A: *C. pallidicaule* is uniformly susceptible to all *P. variabilis* isolates.\n**Implication:** Cannot study ETI/HR; pathosystem limited to disease process studies.\n**Contingency:** (i) Screen wild *Chenopodium* species (*C. berlandieri*, *C. rubrum*, *C. ficifolium*) for resistance sources (Nolen et al., 2022 reported resistance in several *Chenopodium* spp.). (ii) Use *P. syringae* pv. *aptata* or DC3000, which may encounter resistance in *C. pallidicaule* due to evolutionary novelty. (iii) Explore induced resistance (SAR, PR proteins) rather than R-gene-mediated HR.\n\n### Scenario B: A novel, highly aggressive *P. variabilis* isolate emerges in *C. pallidicaule* fields.\n**Implication:** New virulence group beyond V1–V4; potential agricultural threat.\n**Contingency:** Characterize immediately as a new virulence group (e.g., V5); this becomes a valuable resource for studying effector diversity and pathogen evolution. Deposit in culture collection with full documentation.\n\n### Scenario C: *C. pallidicaule* shows strong HR to all tested *P. variabilis* isolates.\n**Implication:** Strong resistance exists; candidate for resistance gene cloning.\n**Contingency:** Use the least virulent isolate that still causes limited infection (e.g., V1 on a susceptible quinoa line co-inoculated with *C. pallidicaule*) to \"prime\" the system, then identify the R gene via BAC library screening or RNA-seq of differentially expressed genes at early hpi (6–12 h).\n\n---\n\n## 11. JUSTIFICATION OF THE BEST PATHOVAR(S)\n\n### 11.1 Primary Recommendation: *Peronospora variabilis* Virulence Group 4 (V4)\n\n**For investigating disease processes (compatible interaction, susceptibility mechanisms, early infection biology):**\n\n| Justification Element | Detail |\n|----------------------|--------|\n| **Broadest host range within *C. pallidicaule*** | V4 overcomes R1, R2, and R3—the three resistance factors identified in quinoa. Unless *C. pallidicaule* carries a functional R4 (unlikely given that V4 has been detected in multiple continents and has been evolving independently in quinoa-growing regions), it will be uniformly susceptible. This guarantees a robust, easily scored disease phenotype. |\n| **Agricultural relevance** | V4 is the most devastating virulence group in quinoa, causing near-total yield loss in susceptible cultivars (Colque-Little et al., 2021). Understanding how *C. pallidicaule* responds to V4 directly informs whether this crop can be recommended for V4-endemic regions. |\n| **Wide availability** | V4 isolates are the most commonly isolated virulence group in Ecuador, Spain, and the USA (Fondevilla et al., 2023; Testen et al., 2014). Isolates can be obtained from existing quinoa research collections. |\n| **Contrast with resistant interactions** | By comparing V4-compatible interactions with V1-incompatible interactions (on resistant *C. pallidicaule* accessions), one can dissect both sides of the host–pathogen equation within a single experimental framework. |\n| **High sporulation** | V4 isolates are the most aggressive and produce the highest sporulation loads, ensuring a reliable, abundant inoculum supply for repeated experiments. |\n\n### 11.2 Secondary Recommendation: *Peronospora variabilis* Virulence Group 1 (V1) or a *C. pallidicaule*-Adapted Isolate\n\n**For investigating resistance mechanisms (incompatible interaction, ETI, HR, R-gene function):**\n\n| Justification Element | Detail |\n|----------------------|--------|\n| **Classical gene-for-gene resistance** | V1 is the least virulent group, resisted by R1. If *C. pallidicaule* cv. 'Bol 1.1' carries an R1 ortholog (suggested by its HR-like lesions; Rollano-Peñaloza et al., 2021), the V1 × 'Bol 1.1' interaction will display textbook HR—a rapid, localized programmed cell death that is the hallmark of ETI. |\n| **Genetic tractability of HR** | HR is mediated by NLR receptors and downstream signaling components (CAMTA, EDS1, PAD4, SAG101, etc.). Studying HR in *C. pallidicaule* will identify orthologs of well-characterized *Arabidopsis* HR genes and may reveal novel, lineage-specific components. |\n| **Host-adapted isolate as novel pathovar** | An isolate originally collected from *C. pallidicaule* fields in Bolivia (e.g., the \"Kari\" isolate of Rollano-Peñaloza et al., 2021) may represent a new virulence group that has specifically adapted to *C. pallidicaule*. Such an isolate would deploy a unique effector repertoire tailored to suppress *C. pallidicaule*-specific defenses, providing a rich resource for effector biology and host-jump evolution studies. |\n\n### 11.3 Complementary Bacterial Pathovar: *Pseudomonas syringae* pv. *aptata* Strain P21\n\n**For molecular dissection requiring superior genetic tools:**\n\n| Justification Element | Detail |\n|----------------------|--------|\n| **Amaranthaceae adaptation** | Naturally infects beet, chard, and spinach; high probability of compatibility with *C. pallidicaule* based on phylogenetic proximity (Ranković et al., 2023). |\n| **T3SS effector toolkit** | Strain P21 carries 15–25 Type III effectors including AvrRpm1, HopAW1, HopAU1, HopM1, and AvrE1. These effectors can be individually deleted, tagged, or heterologously expressed to dissect their functions in suppression of *C. pallidicaule* immunity. |\n| **Genetic manipulability** | Transformable via tri-parental mating; transposon mutagenesis libraries can be constructed; CRISPR-Cas9 genome editing is feasible. The D36E effectorless polymutant (adapted from DC3000; Wei et al., 2015) provides a clean background for effector functional analysis. |\n| **Hemibiotrophic lifestyle** | Engages both SA-dependent (biotrophic phase) and JA/ET-dependent (necrotrophic phase) immunity, complementing the SA-dominated biotroph response and providing a more complete picture of the plant immune system. |\n\n### 11.4 Why Not Other Candidates?\n\n| Candidate | Key Limitation |\n|-----------|---------------|\n| *Botrytis cinerea* | Necrotrophic; kills tissue before feeding; engages JA/ET rather than SA/ETI pathways; less useful for studying gene-for-gene resistance. |\n| *P. syringae* pv. *tomato* DC3000 | Not a natural Chenopodiaceae pathogen; may encounter strong non-host resistance in *C. pallidicaule*; requires wound inoculation or *N. benthamiana* surrogate. |\n| *Albugo* spp. | Mostly restricted to Brassicaceae; *Albugo occidentalis* infects *C. capitatum* but is poorly characterized. |\n| Viruses (e.g., *Cucumber mosaic virus*) | Require vector transmission; slower cycling; less amenable to rapid, high-throughput virulence screening. |\n| *Peronospora effusa* (spinach downy mildew) | Highly host-specific to *Spinacia oleracea*; unlikely to infect *Chenopodium* without prior adaptation. |\n\n---\n\n## 12. EXPECTED OUTCOMES AND SIGNIFICANCE\n\n### 12.1 Short-term (Months 1–6)\n\n1. **Validated, reproducible inoculation protocol** for *P. variabilis* on *C. pallidicaule*, including optimized spore concentration, humidity duration, and temperature regime.\n2. **Virulence profile map** of 10–20 *P. variabilis* isolates on 20–30 *C. pallidicaule* accessions, identifying the most aggressive isolates and the most resistant/susceptible genotypes.\n3. **Designation of at least one reference pathovar** (V4-type isolate) that is consistently virulent on *C. pallidicaule*—this becomes the standard inoculum for all future studies.\n4. **Identification of resistant *C. pallidicaule* accessions** showing HR or tolerance, providing starting material for resistance genetics.\n\n### 12.2 Medium-term (Months 6–36)\n\n5. **Transcriptomic atlas** of compatible and incompatible interactions at key time points post-inoculation.\n6. **Identification of candidate RxLR effector genes** from *P. variabilis* expressed during infection of *C. pallidicaule*.\n7. **Mapping and cloning of resistance QTL/gene(s)** in *C. pallidicaule* using biparental populations.\n8. **Functional validation** of at least one R gene and one Avr gene through transient overexpression, VIGS, or stable transformation.\n\n### 12.3 Long-term (Years 3–5)\n\n9. **Transfer of resistance from *C. pallidicaule* to quinoa** through bridging breeding or gene editing.\n10. **Understanding host-jump evolution**: how *P. variabilis* adapts to new *Chenopodium* hosts as cañahua cultivation expands.\n11. **Establishment of *C. pallidicaule* as a permanent model system** for studying biotrophic oomycete–plant interactions in a diploid, genetically tractable Amaranthaceae crop, comparable in utility to *Arabidopsis*–*H. arabidopsidis*.\n\n---\n\n## 13. SUMMARY TABLE\n\n| Element | Recommendation |\n|---------|---------------|\n| **Primary model pathogen** | *Peronospora variabilis* (oomycete, downy mildew) |\n| **Secondary/complementary pathogen** | *Pseudomonas syringae* pv. *aptata* strain P21 (bacterium, bacterial leaf spot) |\n| **Host species** | *Chenopodium pallidicaule* (diploid, genome-sequenced, halophytic) |\n| **Best pathovar for disease studies** | V4 isolate (overcomes R1–R3; most aggressive; broadly virulent) |\n| **Best pathovar for resistance studies** | V1 isolate (resisted by R1 ortholog in *C. pallidicaule*) or *C. pallidicaule*-adapted isolate (potential novel pathovar) |\n| **Quick virulence screening method** | Leaf-disk assay with spore suspension (1 × 10⁶ spores/mL), 24 h humidity, scoring at 9–12 dpi; dose-response curves for EC₅₀ |\n| **Pathovar determination method** | Cross-inoculation of differential quinoa set (ECU-288, ECU-291, ECU-270, ECU-379) + *C. pallidicaule* accessions; molecular barcoding (ITS + COX2) |\n| **Key experimental phases** | (I) Pathosystem establishment (weeks 1–4), (II) Virulence/host-range screening (weeks 5–12), (III) Pathovar determination (weeks 8–18), (IV) Molecular dissection (months 6–36) |\n| **Expected key outcome** | A well-characterized, stable pathosystem with defined pathovars, ready for genetic and molecular analysis of plant immunity in an underexplored halophytic crop |\n\n---\n\n## REFERENCES\n\n1.
