Unraveling quinoa defense against downy mildew (*Peronospora variabilis*): comparative molecular analysis of resistant \"Hualhuas\" and susceptible \"Real\" cultivars. *Plants*, 13(23), 3344.\n\n---\n\n## SELF-Assessment\n\n**Summary:** The most suitable model pathogen for establishing a rapid, robust pathosystem in *Chenopodium pallidicaule* is *Peronospora variabilis* (downy mildew, obligate biotroph)—confirmed to naturally infect the crop, with a 9–11 day infection cycle, established virulence groups (V1–V4), and existing differential host sets. Virulence Group 4 (V4) is recommended as the best pathovar for studying disease processes (robust compatible interaction), while V1 or a *C. pallidicaule*-adapted isolate is recommended for resistance mechanism studies. A three-tier screening pipeline (quarantine → leaf-disk microassay → full-plant confirmation) enables rapid virulence quantification within 3–4 weeks. *Pseudomonas syringae* pv. *aptata* (strain P21) is recommended as a complementary bacterial model for molecular studies requiring superior genetic tools.\n\n**Confidence Level:** **Medium-High** — The primary recommendation is grounded in peer-reviewed evidence of natural infection (Rollano-Peñaloza et al., 2021), established virulence classification (Ochoa et al., 1999; Colque-Little et al., 2021), and well-characterized inoculation protocols. However, the following caveats apply: (i) the broader field epidemiology of *P. variabilis* on *C. pallidicaule* remains understudied; (ii) the conservation of quinoa R-gene specificity in *C. pallidicaule* must be empirically verified; (iii) *P. syringae* pv. *aptata* compatibility with *C. pallidicaule* is predicted but unconfirmed; and (iv) molecular effector resources for *P. variabilis* are still developing compared to the fully realized *H. arabidopsidis*–*Arabidopsis* toolkit.\n\n**Key Uncertainty:** Whether *C. pallidicaule* will exhibit uniform susceptibility or partial resistance across *P. variabilis* virulence groups—and whether it carries functional R-gene orthologs recognizing specific *P. variabilis* effectors. This can only be resolved through the proposed screening protocol, which is designed explicitly to generate this information.\n\n[Research Report 4]\n# Establishing a Robust Pathosystem in *Chenopodium pallidicaule* for Deciphering Plant Immunity\n\n## Model Pathogen Selection, Virulence Screening, and Pathovar Determination\n\n---\n\n## EXECUTIVE SUMMARY\n\n**Primary model pathogen recommendation:** ***Peronospora variabilis*** Gäum. (oomycete, Peronosporaceae), the causal agent of quinoa downy mildew, is the most suitable primary model pathogen for establishing a rapid, robust pathosystem in *Chenopodium pallidicaule* Aellen. This recommendation is grounded in the single most critical criterion for speed: ***P. variabilis* is the only candidate pathogen for which natural infection of *C. pallidicaule* has been experimentally documented** (Rollano-Peñaloza et al., 2021). The pathogen infects three cañahua varieties, produces classic downy mildew symptoms, and its identity was confirmed by PCR and Sanger sequencing. Furthermore, *P. variabilis* supports both compatible (susceptible cultivar 'Real') and incompatible (hypersensitive response in cultivar 'Bol 1.1'; tolerant cultivar 'Kurmi') interactions, providing the dual readout essential for immune dissection. Four virulence groups and three resistance factors have already been characterized (Ochoa et al., 1999), providing an immediate framework for pathotyping.\n\n**Complementary systems:** *Botrytis cinerea* (necrotrophic ascomycete with world-class genetic tools) and *Pseudomonas syringae* pv. *aptata* (bacterial hemibiotroph with a formal pathovar system and natural Chenopodiaceae affinity) are recommended as secondary and tertiary models, respectively.\n\n**Timeline to robust pathosystem:** ~14–16 weeks from isolate acquisition to a validated, reproducible protocol, with molecular dissection extending to 12 months.\n\n**Key operational definition:** For *P. variabilis*, the equivalent of \"pathovar\" is **\"isolate\"** or **\"virulence group\"** — no formal formae speciales or pathovars have been described within this oomycete species. The selection process therefore focuses on identifying the most aggressive, genetically distinguishable, and reproducible isolate(s) for experimental use.\n\n---\n\n## 1. INTRODUCTION\n\n### 1.1 The Crop and the Challenge\n\n*Chenopodium pallidicaule* Aellen (cañihua/kañihua, 2n = 2x = 18, genome size ~363 Mbp with 22,832 annotated gene models; Mangelson et al., 2019), is a halophytic diploid member of the family Amaranthaceae (subfamily Chenopodioideae, formerly Chenopodiaceae). It is a semi-domesticated Andean pseudocereal closely related to the allotetraploid quinoa (*C. quinoa*, AABB, 2n = 4x = 36). *C. pallidicaule* possesses exceptional stress-tolerance traits — frost, drought, and saline soil tolerance — making it a prime candidate for climate-resilient crop production. However, its systematic deployment to new environments will expose the crop to novel biotic pressures, including adapted pathogens from related *Chenopodium* species and generalist pathogens from adjacent ecosystems. Understanding the plant immune system of *C. pallidicaule* is therefore an urgent prerequisite for its domestication and genetic improvement.\n\nThe central challenge is to establish a **robust, tractable pathosystem** — a compatible host–pathogen interaction yielding measurable disease — **as quickly as possible**, enabling downstream molecular dissection of immune mechanisms. Speed is paramount because every month spent adapting or selecting pathogens is a month delayed in understanding disease susceptibility and resistance.\n\n### 1.2 Guiding Principles for Pathogen Selection\n\nThe following criteria were prioritized, in descending order of importance for the \"speed\" mandate:\n\n1. **Natural infection of *C. pallidicaule*** — the pathogen must already recognize and complete at least part of its life cycle on the crop, eliminating the need for host-range expansion or adaptive evolution.\n2. **Support for both compatible and incompatible interactions** — essential for dissecting both susceptibility mechanisms (biotrophy, effector secretion) and resistance mechanisms (PTI, ETI, hypersensitive response).\n3. **Rapid, quantifiable assay format** — measurable disease symptoms within days, not weeks; reproducible across replicates.\n4. **Availability of genetic tools** — sequenced genome, mutant libraries, or at minimum transcriptomic resources for both pathogen and host.\n5. **Relevance to crop protection** — the pathosystem should model a real field threat.\n6. **Bridge value to *Arabidopsis thaliana*** — ability to leverage the molecular toolkit and literature corpus developed for the Arabidopsis model system.\n\n### 1.3 Scope of This Report\n\nThis report provides:\n- A detailed justification for the primary and complementary model pathogen recommendations\n- An explicit treatment of the \"pathovar\" concept as it applies to each candidate\n- A complete rapid virulence screening protocol\n- Phase-gated experimental steps with timelines and expected outcomes\n- A layered reasoning chain linking evidence to conclusions\n- Discussion of uncertainties, confounders, and falsification experiments\n\n---\n\n## 2. MODEL PATHOGEN SELECTION\n\n### 2.1 Candidate Pathogens Considered\n\nFive candidate pathogen groups were evaluated systematically:\n\n| # | Pathogen | Trophic Strategy | Key Reference |\n|---|----------|-----------------|---------------|\n| 1 | *Peronospora variabilis* Gäum. | Obligate biotrophic oomycete | Rollano-Peñaloza et al. (2021, 2022) |\n| 2 | *Botrytis cinerea* Pers.: Fr. Tuell & de Hoog | Generalist necrotrophic ascomycete | Zhu et al. (2025); Colque-Little et al. (2021) |\n| 3 | *Pseudomonas syringae* (E. F. Smith) Knapp | Hemibiotrophic bacterium | Fonseca-Guerra et al. (2021); Baltrus et al. (2011) |\n| 4 | *Sclerotinia sclerotiorum* (Lib.) de Bary | Necrotrophic ascomycete | Mangwende et al. (2025) |\n| 5 | *Colletotrichum* spp. (Corda.) J.H. Simmons | Hemibiotrophic ascomycete | Colque-Little et al. (2021) |\n\n### 2.2 Weighted Decision Matrix\n\nA multi-criterion decision analysis was performed using nine weighted criteria, each scored on a 0–5 scale (5 = excellent). Three weighting scenarios were tested:\n\n**Table 1 — Weighted Decision Matrix Results**\n\n| Scenario | Rank 1 | Score | Rank 2 | Score | Rank 3 | Score |\n|----------|--------|-------|--------|-------|--------|-------|\n| Primary (balanced) | *B. cinerea* | 4.05 | *P. syringae* | 3.94 | *P. variabilis* | 3.79 |\n| Genetic tools priority | *P. syringae* | 4.80 | *B. cinerea* | 4.64 | *S. sclerotiorum* | 3.54 |\n| **Natural infection + crop protection** | ***P. variabilis*** | **4.07** | *B. cinerea* | 3.84 | *P. syringae* | 3.71 |\n\nThe primary (balanced) scenario produces a close race between *B. cinerea* and *P. syringae*, with *P. variabilis* a close third. However, the **natural infection + crop protection scenario** — which reflects the criteria most relevant to the \"as quickly as possible\" mandate — ranks *P. variabilis* unambiguously first. The decisive factor is that *P. variabilis* is the **only candidate with documented natural infection of *C. pallidicaule***, which carries the highest weight (0.18) and is scored 5.0 only by *P. variabilis*.\n\n### 2.3 Primary Recommendation: *Peronospora variabilis*\n\n#### 2.3.1 Taxonomy and Nomenclature\n\n*Peronospora variabilis* Gäum. (syn. *Peronospora farinosa* f. sp. *chenopodii* Byford.) is an obligate biotrophic oomycete in the family Peronosporaceae (order Peronosporales). The species was formerly treated as a formae speciales on *Chenopodium* but was reinstated as a distinct species by Gäumann and later confirmed molecularly by Thines et al. (2016) and Testen et al. (2014). The pathogen is host-specific to *Chenopodium* species, with *C. quinoa* and *C. pallidicaule* as primary crop hosts and *C. album* L. (common lambsquarters) as an important weed reservoir host (Colque-Little et al., 2021).\n\n#### 2.3.2 Evidence for Natural Infection of *C. pallidicaule*\n\nThe foundational evidence comes from Rollano-Peñaloza et al. (2021), who reported the **first occurrence of *P. variabilis* causing downy mildew on cañahua (*C. pallidicaule*) in Bolivia**. Key findings:\n\n- In May 2018, cañahua plants in Bolivia exhibited classic downy mildew symptoms: chlorosis and sporulation on abaxial leaf surfaces.\n- Microscopic confirmation of *P. variabilis* reproductive structures (sporangiophores and sporangia) was obtained from symptomatic tissue.\n- **Artificial inoculation of three cañahua varieties** with a *P. variabilis* sporangiospore suspension (1 × 10⁶ sporangia/mL) resulted in downy mildew disease symptoms in all three varieties.\n- **Pathogen identity was confirmed by PCR and Sanger sequencing** of the PvCox2 and PvITS regions, showing 99.8% and 100% identity, respectively, to *P. variabilis* isolates from quinoa.\n- DNA sequence identification confirmed that **the same *P. variabilis* population that infects quinoa can infect cañahua.**\n\nThis single study eliminates the most significant barrier to rapid pathosystem establishment: **no pathogen adaptation or host-range expansion is required.**\n\n#### 2.3.3 Documented Compatible and Incompatible Interactions\n\nRollano-Peñaloza et al. (2022) characterized the disease progression of the **\"Kari\" isolate** of *P. variabilis* on two quinoa cultivars with contrasting tolerance:\n\n- **Susceptible cultivar 'Real':** Showed heavy sporulation from 7 dpi, severe wilting, early flowering (stress-induced), and high proportions of dead leaves by 21 dpi.\n- **Tolerant cultivar 'Kurmi':** Exhibited more pronounced initial chlorosis but better overall tolerance, with localized sporulation restricted to chlorotic areas, continued main-stem leaf production, and no early flowering.\n- **Hypersensitive response (HR):** Observed in the cañahua cultivar 'Bol 1.1' upon infection (Rollano-Peñaloza et al., 2021), indicating an incompatible interaction and the presence of resistance (R) gene recognition.\n\nThese interactions provide the **dual readout essential for immune dissection**: susceptible interactions reveal susceptibility mechanisms (haustorial feeding, effector secretion, suppression of plant defenses), while incompatible interactions (HR) reveal recognition events (PTI/ETI).\n\n#### 2.3.4 Existing Genetic Resources\n\n**Pathogen resources:**\n- Molecular characterization using COX1, COX2, and ITS barcodes (Fondevilla et al., 2023; Nolen et al., 2022; Testen et al., 2014).\n- Mitochondrial genome assembly available (GenBank MT895880).\n- Transcriptome sequencing performed (Rollano-Peñaloza et al., 2022).\n- Four virulence groups (VG1–VG4) and three resistance factors (R1, R3) defined by Ochoa et al. (1999) using differential quinoa accessions.\n- Evidence for race-specific variation: Colque-Little et al. (2021) identified four virulence groups based on differential infection of quinoa accessions; Khalifa & Thabet (2018) assessed downy mildew resistance variation in quinoa and kañiwa under Egyptian conditions.\n\n**Host resources:**\n- Chromosome-scale reference genome for *C. pallidicaule*: ~363 Mbp, 9 chromosomes (2n = 2x = 18), 22,832 annotated gene models (Mangelson et al., 2019).\n- Quinoa genome (allotetraploid, AABB, 2n = 4x = 36) sequenced to high quality (Jarvis et al., 2017).\n- Quinoa orthologs of Arabidopsis defense genes characterized: CqWRKY33, CqHSP83, CqCAT2, CqEP3, CqPR4 (Rollano-Peñaloza et al., 2022).\n- Quinoa resistance to *P. variabilis* governed by both major (vertical) and minor (horizontal) genes, with QTLs mapped (Colque-Little et al., 2021; Maldonado-Taipe et al., 2022).\n\n#### 2.3.5 Practical Advantages for Rapid Setup\n\n- **Seed-transmitted:** Oospores survive in seeds and soil, ensuring pathogen maintenance across generations.\n- **Greenhouse-culturable:** Simple inoculation under high-humidity conditions (>85% RH) at 22 ± 2°C.\n- **Rapid disease development:** Symptoms appear within 2–9 days post-inoculation (Rollano-Peñaloza et al., 2022).\n- **No special biosafety restrictions:** Not a regulated pathogen in most countries; BSL-1.\n- **Maintainable on quinoa cv. 'Real':** Serial transfer every two weeks with propiconazole (25 μg/mL) added to sporangia wash to suppress superimposed infections (Rollano-Peñaloza et al., 2022).\n\n#### 2.3.6 Limitations\n\n- **Obligate biotroph:** Cannot be cultured axenically; requires living host plants for maintenance. This precludes the generation of auxotrophic mutants and limits metabolic studies.\n- **No reference genome:** Transcriptome assemblies exist but a chromosome-scale genome is lacking, complicating effector discovery and population genetics.\n- **Does not infect *Arabidopsis*:** The conceptual bridge to Arabidopsis is limited to oomycete biology (haustorial infection, RxLR effector families, downy mildew resistance genes) rather than direct cross-infection.\n- **Controlled environment requirements:** High humidity (>95% for 24 h post-inoculation) and temperature control (17–25°C) are essential for reproducible infection.\n\n### 2.4 Secondary Recommendation: *Botrytis cinerea*\n\n*B. cinerea* is a cosmopolitan necrotrophic fungus with a host range exceeding 1,000 species across >130 families. It is the **premier model necrotroph** for plant pathology:\n\n- **Documented infection of *C. album*:** Zhu et al. (2025) demonstrated that *B. cinerea* strain HZ-011 (isolated from *Rumex patientia*, Amaranthaceae) causes progressive necrotic lesions on *C. album*, suppressing photosynthetic gene expression and killing the plant within 5 days post-inoculation. This provides direct evidence of compatibility within the genus.\n- **World-class genetic toolkit:** Fully sequenced genome (Bc5.0, ~35 Mb, 10 chromosomes; Ensembl Fungi); T-DNA insertion mutant library (>14,000 transformants); characterized effectors (BcSPD1, Bc16Glyco, BcCDI1), phytotoxins (botrydial), and cell-wall-degrading enzymes.\n- **Rapid, quantifiable assay:** Detached-leaf droplet assay with 5–6 μL of 10⁵ conidia/mL; lesions visible within 24–48 h; lesion diameter measured by ImageJ at 48–72 hpi.\n- **Bridges to *Arabidopsis*:** Extensive literature on *Arabidopsis*–*B. cinerea* interactions covering JA/ET signaling, ROS bursts, programmed cell death, and SA/JA antagonism.\n\n**Limitations:** Not specifically adapted to *Chenopodium*; may require wounding for consistent infection. No formal pathovar system. Necrotrophic lifestyle studies JA/ET pathways rather than SA-mediated biotroph resistance — complementary rather than redundant with *P. variabilis*.\n\n**Recommendation:** Establish *B. cinerea* as a parallel secondary pathosystem, using strain HZ-011 or a well-characterized laboratory strain (e.g., T4, M712) as the starting point, with pre-screening of 5–10 Amaranthaceae-origin isolates.\n\n### 2.5 Tertiary Recommendation: *Pseudomonas syringae* pv. *aptata*\n\n*P. syringae* is the most extensively studied plant-pathogenic bacterium. The species complex comprises >60 formally described pathovars with distinct host ranges spanning >180 plant species (Lindeberg et al., 2009; Baltrus et al., 2011).\n\n**Specific rationale for pv. *aptata*:**\n- **Natural host includes *Beta vulgaris*** (sugar beet, Swiss chard), members of the same subfamily (Chenopodioideae) and phylogenetically the closest crop relatives of *Chenopodium*.\n- **Preliminary evidence of infection on *C. album*:** Strains of *P. syringae* pv. *aptata* pathogenic on beet and chard can cause leaf spot on common lambsquarters (*C. album*).\n- **Formal pathovar system:** >60 pathovars distinguished by host range, pathogenicity, and MLSA profiles — providing a natural framework for the \"pathovar determination\" question.\n- **Unmatched bacterial genetic tools:** *Pst* DC3000 (pv. *tomato*) genome sequenced (5.76 Mb); complete transposon mutagenesis libraries; Δ28E mutant lacking all confirmed T3 effectors.\n- **Hemibiotrophic lifestyle:** Early biotrophic phase (T3SS effector injection, PTI suppression) and late necrotrophic phase (phytotoxins, CWDEs) allow study of both immune evasion and cell death regulation.\n\n**Limitations:** No confirmed natural infection of *C. pallidicaule*. Non-host resistance may block infection. First report of *P. syringae* on quinoa is from Colombia (Fonseca-Guerra et al., 2021), where the pathovar was not determined.\n\n**Recommendation:** Screen a panel of six *P. syringae* pathovars (pv. *aptata*, pv. *tomato* DC3000, pv. *phaseolicola* 1448a, pv. *syringae* B728a, pv. *glycinea* R4, pv. *maculicola*), with pv. *aptata* and DC3000 as priority candidates.\n\n### 2.6 Why Not Other Candidates?\n\n| Pathogen | Reason for Rejection as Primary |\n|----------|-------------------------------|\n| *Hyaloperonospora arabidopsidis* | Obligate biotroph with extremely narrow host range (Brassicaceae only); will not infect *C. pallidicaule*. |\n| *Sclerotinia sclerotiorum* | Necrotroph requiring wounding; slower disease development (5–10 days); less suited for R-gene studies. |\n| *Colletotrichum* spp. | Hemibiotrophic fungi with moderate genetic tools; longer incubation (7–14 days); formae speciales less well-defined. |\n| *Alternaria alternata* | Necrotroph with host-specific toxins; weak genetic tools; primarily opportunistic. |\n| *Fusarium* spp. | Soil-borne wilt pathogens; slow disease development (7–14 days); require soil-based assays. |\n| Tobamoviruses / CMV | Viruses differ fundamentally in pathogenesis (no haustorial interface); require different expertise. |\n\n---\n\n## 3. THE \"PATHOVAR\" CONCEPT IN CHENOPODIUM PATHOGENS\n\n### 3.1 Formal Definitions\n\nThe term **pathovar** (*pathovarietas*, abbreviated *pv.*) is formally defined by the International Society for Plant Pathology (ISPP Standard 5) as \"a strain or set of strains with the same or similar characteristics, differentiated at infrasubspecific level from other strains of the same species or subspecies on the basis of distinctive pathogenicity to one or more plant hosts.\" Pathovars are primarily distinguished by proved differences in host range (Young et al., 1996). For fungi and oomycetes, the equivalent infrasubspecific rank is **formas speciales** (f. sp., plural *formae speciales*).\n\n### 3.2 Application to Each Candidate\n\n#### 3.2.1 *Peronospora variabilis* — No Formal Pathovars; \"Isolate\" or \"Virulence Group\"\n\n*P. variabilis* was formerly classified as *Peronospora farinosa* f. sp. *chenopodii* Byford. The species-level reclassification (Gäumann, 1919; confirmed molecularly by Thines et al., 2016) means it is treated as a distinct species with a host range restricted to *Chenopodium*. **No formal formae speciales or pathovars have been described within *P. variabilis***.\n\nInstead, diversity is captured at the **isolate** or **virulence group** level:\n- Ochoa et al. (1999) defined four virulence groups (VG1–VG4) and three resistance factors (R1, R3) using 60 Ecuadorian isolates tested against differential quinoa accessions.\n- Fondevilla et al. (2023) showed genetic uniformity among Spanish isolates but distinguished them from South American isolates using COX1 and COX2 barcodes.\n- Nolen et al. (2022) found that COX2 sequences of *P. variabilis* isolates did not cluster by host species (*C. quinoa* vs. *C. album*), suggesting limited host specialization at the molecular level.\n- Rollano-Peñaloza et al. (2022) characterized individual isolates (e.g., \"Kari\" isolate from Bolivian quinoa) with distinct disease progression kinetics.\n\n**Operational translation:** When this report refers to \"selecting the best pathovar\" of *P. variabilis*, it means **selecting the most suitable isolate(s)** based on virulence, reproducibility, genetic distinguishability, and availability of an avirulent counterpart.\n\n#### 3.2.2 *Pseudomonas syringae* — Formal Pathovar System\n\n*P. syringae* possesses the most rigorously developed pathovar system among plant pathogens. Over 60 validly published pathovars are recognized, grouped into 13 phylogroups based on MLSA (Lindeberg et al., 2009). Pathovar assignment requires: host range characterization, DNA-DNA hybridization or ANI analysis, MLSA profile comparison, deposit of type strain in two international culture collections, and publication in IJSEM (Young et al., 1996).\n\n#### 3.2.3 *Botrytis cinerea* — No Pathovars; Strain-Level Diversity\n\n*B. cinerea* does not possess formal pathovars or formae speciales. Host association studies (Valero-Jiménez et al., 2019) show that populations often cluster by host, but the species is classified as a \"generalist\" with extreme genetic variability. The equivalent of \"pathovar\" for *B. cinerea* is **\"strain\"** or **\"isolate.\"**\n\n### 3.3 Implications for Pathovar Determination\n\n| Pathogen | Equivalent Rank | Selection Method |\n|----------|----------------|------------------|\n| *P. variabilis* | Isolate / Virulence Group | Differential infection panel; molecular barcoding (COX1, COX2, ITS); AUDPC ranking |\n| *P. syringae* | Pathovar (formal) | Host range testing; MLSA; effector gene profiling; whole-genome sequencing |\n| *B. cinerea* | Strain / Isolate | Lesion size assay; host range check; transformation efficiency; stability over passage |\n\n---\n\n## 4. RAPID VIRULENCE SCREENING PROTOCOL FOR *Peronospora variabilis*\n\n### 4.1 Objective\n\nTo quickly identify the most aggressive, reproducible, and genetically distinguishable isolate(s) of *P. variabilis* that cause consistent, measurable disease on *C. pallidicaule*, and simultaneously identify isolates that are excluded (avirulent) for studying resistance mechanisms.\n\n### 4.2 Isolate Collection and Acquisition\n\n**Sources (Target: 15–20 isolates):**\n\n| Source | Rationale | Estimated Isolates |\n|--------|-----------|-------------------|\n| *C. pallidicaule* fields in Bolivia/Peru | Native pathogen, already adapted to crop | 5–8 |\n| *C. quinoa* fields (Bolivia, Peru, Ecuador, Spain, USA) | Close host relationship; high probability of compatibility | 5–8 |\n| *C. album* stands in quinoa/cañahua fields | Weed reservoir host; sympatric isolation | 3–5 |\n| Culture collections (APS, CBS, CFBP) | Verified identities; some with known host specificity | 2–4 |\n\nEach isolate is maintained separately on susceptible quinoa cv. 'Real' under greenhouse conditions, with propiconazole (25 μg/mL) added to sporangia wash to prevent superimposed infections (Rollano-Peñaloza et al., 2022).\n\n### 4.3 Inoculum Preparation\n\n1. Collect sporulating quinoa leaves (abaxial surface with visible dark grey sporulation).\n2. Wash leaves in cold distilled water containing 0.1% Tween-20, agitating gently.\n3. Filter through cheesecloth or Miracloth to remove debris.\n4. Add propiconazole (25 μg/mL) to prevent fungal contamination.\n5. Count sporangia using a hemocytometer; adjust to 1 × 10⁵, 1 × 10⁶, and 1 × 10⁷ sporangia/mL.\n6. Verify viability by plating on Oomycete Select Medium (OSM) or potato dextrose agar (PDA).\n\n### 4.4 Plant Material Preparation\n\n1. Sow *C. pallidicaule* seeds (multiple accessions: Sayhua, Lasta, Phajwa types, plus 'Bol 1.1', 'Kurmi') in sterile potting mix.\n2. Grow under greenhouse conditions: 22 ± 2°C, 16/8 h light/dark, high humidity (>70%).\n3. Use 4–6 true-leaf stage plants (approximately 3–4 weeks after germination).\n4. Include susceptible quinoa cv. 'Real' as positive control and mock-inoculated plants as negative control.\n\n### 4.5 Spray Inoculation Assay — Primary Screening\n\n**Step 1 — Inoculation:**\n- Place plants in mist chamber or cover with transparent plastic domes to maintain >95% RH.\n- Spray inoculum onto leaves until runoff, ensuring both abaxial and adaxial surfaces are wetted.\n- Maintain high humidity for 6 h darkness (critical for sporangial germination and penetration).\n- Each isolate × host combination: n ≥ 10 plants.\n- Include non-inoculated control (water + 0.1% Tween-20).\n\n**Step 2 — Disease Scoring:**\n\nScore disease severity at 3, 5, 7, 10, and 14 days post-inoculation (dpi) using the following standardized scale:\n\n| Score | Symptom Description | Sporulation |\n|-------|---------------------|-------------|\n| 0 | No visible symptoms | None |\n| 1 | Small chlorotic spots (<2 mm), few in number | None |\n| 2 | Chlorotic spots 2–5 mm, moderate number; some leaf curling | None or minimal |\n| 3 | Extensive chlorosis/necrosis (>25% leaf area); visible sporulation | Sporodochia visible |\n| 4 | Severe necrosis (>50% leaf area); heavy sporulation; plant wilting | Abundant sporulation |\n| 5 | Plant death; complete sporulation coverage | Massive sporulation |\n\n**Step 3 — Hypersensitive Response Assessment:**\nAt 48–72 hpi, stain leaf discs with iodine-potassium iodide (IKI) or trypan blue to detect HR (localized cell death manifesting as small, water-soaked spots that turn dark upon staining).\n\n**Step 4 — Data Analysis:**\n- Count sporodochia (sporulation) on abaxial leaf surface at 7 and 10 dpi (microscopy, 40× magnification).\n- Calculate Area Under the Disease Progress Curve (AUDPC):\n\n$$AUDPC = \\sum_{i=1}^{n-1} \\frac{(x_{i+1} + x_i)}{2} (t_{i+1} - t_i)$$\n\nwhere $x_i$ is disease severity at time $t_i$.\n\n- Perform ANOVA with isolate and host accession as fixed effects.\n- Cluster isolates based on virulence patterns across host accessions.\n\n### 4.6 Complementary Assays for Secondary Pathogens\n\n**For *B. cinerea* — Detached Leaf Droplet Assay:**\n1. Harvest conidia from 7–10 day old PDA cultures; suspend in sterile water + 0.01% Tween-20; filter through glass wool.\n2. Adjust to 1 × 10⁵ conidia/mL.\n3. Deposit 5–6 μL droplets on fully expanded leaves (adaxial or abaxial).\n4. Incubate at 22°C, high humidity, 24 h dark then 22°C/18°C light/dark.\n5. Measure lesion diameter at 24, 48, and 72 hpi using ImageJ.\n\n**For *P. syringae* — Syringe Infiltration Assay:**\n1. Grow bacteria in NGM or KB medium at 28°C to OD₆₀₀ = 0.5.\n2. Adjust to 10⁶, 10⁷, and 10⁸ CFU/mL in 10 mM MgCl₂ + 100 μM acetosyringone.\n3. Infiltrate into abaxial leaf apoplast using blunt-ended 1 mL syringe (no needle).\n4. Score water-soaked lesions at 24, 48, and 72 hpi.\n5. Punch 6-mm leaf discs; homogenize in 1 mL sterile water; serially dilute and plate on NGM + selective antibiotics.\n6. Compute bacterial growth (log₁₀ CFU/mm² leaf area).\n\n### 4.7 Expected Outcomes from Screening\n\n| Outcome | Interpretation |\n|---------|---------------|\n| All *P. variabilis* isolates cause disease on *C. pallidicaule* | Crop is broadly susceptible; select most aggressive isolate for routine use |\n| Some isolates cause disease, others do not | Presence of avirulence factors; useful for resistance studies |\n| Variable severity among isolates | Virulence groups exist; select both highly virulent and weakly virulent isolates for comparative studies |\n| No isolates cause disease | *C. pallidicaule* is resistant; investigate biotic/abiotic factors limiting infection; consider wound inoculation |\n\n---\n\n## 5. DETERMINING THE MOST SUITABLE ISOLATE / PATHOVAR\n\n### 5.1 Selection Criteria\n\n| Criterion | Weight | Desired Property |\n|-----------|--------|------------------|\n| Virulence on *C. pallidicaule* | High | Large, consistent AUDPC within 5–7 dpi |\n| Reproducibility | High | Low variance across biological replicates and experiments |\n| Sporulation productivity | Medium | ≥10⁶ sporangia/mL for repeat experiments |\n| Genetic distinguishability | Medium | Discriminated by molecular markers (COX1, COX2, ITS) |\n| Availability of avirulent counterpart | Medium | An isolate that fails to infect or causes only mild symptoms |\n| Stability over serial passage | Low | Maintains virulence over ≥3 passages |\n| Geographic/ecological relevance | Low | Isolate from center of diversity (Bolivia/Peru) |\n\n### 5.2 Selection Workflow\n\n```\nScreen 15–20 P. variabilis isolates on C. pallidicaule (cv. 'Real' and 'Kurmi')\n         │\n         ▼\nRank by AUDPC at 14 dpi\n         │\n         ├── Most virulent isolate (highest AUDPC on cv. 'Real')\n         │       → Designated \"Isolate V\" (primary working strain)\n         ├── Second most virulent isolate\n         │       → Designated \"Isolate V2\" (for replication and cross-validation)\n         ├── Isolate showing no/low disease on cv. 'Kurmi' or 'Bol 1.1'\n         │       → Designated \"Isolate A\" (avirulent/incompatible counterpart)\n         └── Bolivian/Peruvian isolate from C. pallidicaule field\n                 → Designated \"Isolate L\" (for ecological relevance)\n```\n\n### 5.3 Preliminary Recommendation Based on Published Data\n\n**Primary candidate: \"Kari\" isolate (Rollano-Peñaloza et al., 2022)**\n- Collected from quinoa greenhouse (Bolivian Andean plateau).\n- Well-characterized at molecular level (ITS, COX2 sequencing; disease progression kinetics on cv. Real and Kurmi).\n- Proven virulence on quinoa; expected cross-infection on *C. pallidicaule* given close host relationship (shared A-genome ancestry).\n- Available as a reference isolate for future inter-laboratory comparisons.\n\n**Secondary candidate: Isolate(s) from *C. pallidicaule* fields in Bolivia**\n- Naturally adapted to the crop (Rollano-Peñaloza et al., 2021).\n- Collected from fields where downy mildew is already established, suggesting high fitness.\n- Geographic origin (Bolivia) aligns with crop center of diversity.\n\n**Avirulent counterpart:** The isolate that fails to infect resistant *C. pallidicaule* accessions (e.g., 'Bol 1.1', which showed HR). Alternatively, an isolate from a geographic region distant from the crop's center of diversity, which may encounter stronger non-host resistance.\n\n### 5.4 Formal Pathovar Designation for *Pseudomonas syringae*\n\nIf a *P. syringae* pathovar proves compatible with *C. pallidicaule*:\n1. Comprehensive host range characterization on *C. pallidicaule*, *C. quinoa*, *C. album*, *Beta vulgaris*, *Spinacia oleracea*, *Arabidopsis thaliana*, and selected additional species.\n2. MLSA: sequence rpoD, hrpA, atpD, gyrA, and effector genes (avrPto, avrPtob, hopA1, hopM1, hopAI1).\n3. Whole-genome sequencing for ANI comparison to existing *P. syringae* pathovars.\n4. If the isolate represents a novel pathovar: follow Young et al. (1996) protocol — deposit type strain in two international culture collections, publish description in IJSEM.\n5. If the isolate matches a known pathovar: confirm by effector gene profiling and document host range extension.\n\n---\n\n## 6. LOGICAL EXPERIMENTAL STEPS WITH TIMELINES AND EXPECTED OUTCOMES\n\n### Phase 1: Pathogen Acquisition and Verification (Weeks 1–4)\n\n| Week | Activity | Expected Outcome |\n|------|----------|------------------|\n| 1–2 | Collect sporulating tissue/seeds from *C. pallidicaule*, *C. quinoa*, and *C. album* fields; request cultures from APS, CBS, CFBP | 15–20 active *P. variabilis* isolates; 5–8 *B. cinerea* isolates; 6 *P. syringae* pathovars |\n| 2–3 | Maintain *P. variabilis* on quinoa cv. 'Real' with propiconazole (25 μg/mL); grow *B. cinerea* on PDA; grow *P. syringae* on NGM | Continuous supply of inoculum; glycerol stocks at −80°C |\n| 3–4 | Molecular confirmation: amplify ITS, COX2 (oomycetes), ITS (fungi), 16S rDNA (bacteria); Sanger sequencing; BLAST | ≥99% sequence identity to type strains; sequences deposited in GenBank |\n\n### Phase 2: Rapid Virulence Screening (Weeks 5–8)\n\n| Week | Activity | Expected Outcome |\n|------|----------|------------------|\n| 5–6 | Sow *C. pallidicaule* seeds (≥5 accessions); prepare inoculum from each isolate | Uniform 4–6 leaf-stage plants; standardized suspensions |\n| 6–7 | Primary inoculation: spray (P. variabilis, B. cinerea); syringe infiltration (P. syringae); maintain >95% RH for 24 h | Inoculated plants; controls included |\n| 7–10 | Disease scoring at appropriate intervals per pathogen | Disease severity data; AUDPC values; bacterial growth curves |\n| 10–12 | ANOVA; clustering of isolates by virulence pattern; selection of top 3–5 isolates per pathogen | Ranked isolate list; identification of most virulent and avirulent isolates |\n\n### Phase 3: Pathosystem Validation (Weeks 13–20)\n\n| Week | Activity | Expected Outcome |\n|------|----------|------------------|\n| 13–16 | Repeat best isolate(s) with biological replicates (n = 20 per treatment) | Low-variance, reproducible disease scores |\n| 16–18 | Time-course molecular sampling: harvest leaves at 0, 6, 12, 24, 48, 72 hpi; extract RNA; qRT-PCR for defense genes (CqWRKY33, CqHSP83, CqCAT2, CqEP3) | Baseline immune response kinetics |\n| 18–20 | Environmental optimization: test temperature (15, 20, 25°C), humidity (80, 90, 95% RH), light (0, 12, 16 h photoperiod) | Standardized conditions for routine use |\n| 20–22 | Host range expansion: test on *C. quinoa*, *C. album*, *B. vulgaris*, *S. oleracea*, *A. thaliana* (negative control) | Host range map; confirmation of *Chenopodium*-specific infection |\n\n### Phase 4: Molecular Dissection (Months 5–12)\n\n| Activity | Method | Expected Outcome |\n|----------|--------|------------------|\n| Transcriptome profiling | RNA-seq of *C. pallidicaule* leaves at multiple time points post-inoculation with virulent (Isolate V) and avirulent (Isolate A) isolates | Differential expression of immune genes; PTI/ETI temporal mapping |\n| Effector discovery | RNA-seq of *P. variabilis* during infection; identify secreted effector candidates (RXLR-like, CRN-type via signal peptide prediction) | Candidate effector list for functional validation |\n| Host R-gene candidates | Screen *C. pallidicaule* NBS-LRR gene repertoire for differential expression; screen diverse accessions for resistance | Candidate R-genes; resistance mapping population |\n| Hormone quantification | LC-MS/MS for SA, JA, IAA, ABA at key time points | Hormonal regulation of immune response |\n| Cytological analysis | Light microscopy of stained leaf sections (lactophenol cotton blue) to observe haustoria, hyphae, and HR | Haustorial formation; HR cell death; papillae deposition |\n\n### Phase 5: Complementary Pathosystem Establishment (Parallel, Months 2–6)\n\n| Pathogen | Activity | Timeline |\n|----------|----------|----------|\n| *B. cinerea* | Pre-screen 5–10 Amaranthaceae-origin isolates using detached leaf droplet assay; select best strain; validate on whole plants | Weeks 6–14 |\n| *P. syringae* | Screen 6 pathovars using syringe infiltration; identify compatible pathovar(s); characterize quinoa isolates molecularly | Weeks 6–14 |\n\n---\n\n## 7. LAYERED REASONING CHAIN\n\nEach reasoning node presents a claim, the evidence supporting it, and its logical dependencies.\n\n---\n\n**R₁ — *C. pallidicaule* is naturally susceptible to *P. variabilis*.**\n\n*Claim:* *Peronospora variabilis* naturally infects and causes disease on *Chenopodium pallidicaule*.\n\n*Evidence:* Rollano-Peñaloza et al. (2021) documented downy mildew on cañahua in Bolivia, with microscopic confirmation of *P. variabilis* reproductive structures. Artificial inoculation of three cañahua varieties with *P. variabilis* sporangiospore suspension resulted in disease symptoms in all three. PCR and Sanger sequencing of PvCox2 and PvITS confirmed identity as *P. variabilis* with 99.8% and 100% identity to quinoa isolates.\n\n*Dependencies:* None (foundational observation).\n\n*Confidence:* **High** — multiple lines of evidence converge.\n\n---\n\n**R₂ — *P. variabilis* is the fastest route to a functional pathosystem.**\n\n*Claim:* Because *P. variabilis* already naturally infects *C. pallidicaule*, it eliminates the need for pathogen adaptation, host-range expansion, or selective pressure — processes that can take months to years for other candidates.\n\n*Evidence:* R₁ establishes natural infection. *B. cinerea* has been documented on *C. album* (Zhu et al., 2025) but not specifically on *C. pallidicaule*; pre-screening of multiple isolates is required. *P. syringae* pv. *aptata* infects *Beta* spp. and preliminarily *C. album*, but has not been tested on *C. pallidicaule*; screening of multiple pathovars is required. Both *B. cinerea* and *P. syringae* may require empirical identification of compatible strains/isolates, adding 2–8 weeks to the timeline.\n\n*Dependencies:* R₁.\n\n*Confidence:* **High** — the logic is straightforward: a pathogen that already infects the crop requires less time to establish than one that needs to be screened for compatibility.\n\n---\n\n**R₃ — *P. variabilis* supports both compatible and incompatible interactions.**\n\n*Claim:* The *P. variabilis*–*C. pallidicaule*/*C. quinoa* system offers both susceptible (compatible) and resistant (incompatible) interactions, enabling dissection of both susceptibility and resistance mechanisms.\n\n*Evidence:* Quinoa cv. 'Real' is highly susceptible (heavy sporulation, wilting, early flowering; Rollano-Peñaloza et al., 2022). Quinoa cv. 'Kurmi' is tolerant (localized sporulation, continued growth). Cañahua cv. 'Bol 1.1' exhibited hypersensitive response (HR) upon infection (Rollano-Peñaloza et al., 2021). Four virulence groups and three resistance factors have been defined (Ochoa et al., 1999; Colque-Little et al., 2021). Resistance in 'Kurmi' is associated with constitutive H₂O₂ accumulation, POX/PAL activity, and PR-10 upregulation (Khalifa et al., 2024).\n\n*Dependencies:* R₁.\n\n*Confidence:* **Medium-High** — HR has been observed but not systematically characterized; the molecular basis of resistance in 'Bol 1.1' is unknown.\n\n---\n\n**R₄ — The \"pathovar\" concept for *P. variabilis* translates to \"isolate\" or \"virulence group\".**\n\n*Claim:* Unlike *P. syringae* (which has >60 formal pathovars), *P. variabilis* has no formally described formae speciales or pathovars. Diversity is captured at the isolate/virulence group level through differential infection panels and molecular barcoding.\n\n*Evidence:* *P. variabilis* was formerly *P. farinosa* f. sp. *chenopodii*; species-level reclassification (Gäumann; Thines et al., 2016) rendered the f. sp. designation obsolete. Ochoa et al. (1999) defined four virulence groups using differential quinoa accessions, not formal taxonomic ranks. Fondevilla et al. (2023) and Nolen et al. (2022) characterize isolates by COX1/COX2 sequences, not pathovar designations. EXPECTED OUTCOMES\n\n### 8.1 Short-Term (0–4 Months)\n\n1. **Confirmed list of *P. variabilis* isolates** that are virulent, moderately virulent, and avirulent on *C. pallidicaule*.\n2. **Standardized inoculation protocol** yielding reproducible disease scores (AUDPC values with coefficient of variation <25%).\n3. **Baseline disease severity data** across *C. pallidicaule* accessions, identifying the most susceptible and most resistant germplasm.\n4. **Validated molecular markers** (CqWRKY33, CqHSP83, CqCAT2, CqEP3) for rapid screening in future experiments.\n5. **Operational *B. cinerea* assay** with at least one compatible strain producing lesions in 48–72 h.\n6. **Operational *P. syringae* assay** with at least one compatible pathovar showing bacterial growth and necrotic lesions.\n\n### 8.2 Medium-Term (4–12 Months)\n\n1. **Transcriptomic maps** of the *C. pallidicaule* immune response at early (PTI, 0–12 hpi) and late (ETI, 24–72 hpi) stages.\n2. **Identification of *P. variabilis* candidate effectors** (RxLR-like, CRN-type) that suppress PTI or trigger ETI.\n3. **Characterization of *C. pallidicaule* candidate R-genes** that confer resistance to specific *P. variabilis* isolates.\n4. **Hormonal profiles** (SA, JA, IAA, ABA) at key infection time points via LC-MS/MS.\n5. **Cytological characterization** of haustorial formation, papillae deposition, and HR cell death.\n\n### 8.3 Long-Term (1–3 Years)\n\n1. A **genetically tractable primary pathosystem** (*P. variabilis*) where both host resistance and pathogen virulence can be manipulated.\n2. **Molecular markers for breeding** *C. pallidicaule* varieties with durable downy mildew resistance.\n3. **Comparative immunity insights** across *Chenopodium* species (*C. pallidicaule*, *C. quinoa*, *C. album*, *C. berlandieri*).\n4. **Functional validation of R-gene orthologs** from *C. pallidicaule* in *Arabidopsis* or *N. benthamiana* transient expression systems.\n5. **Integration of necrotroph and bacterial pathosystems** for comprehensive immune profiling.\n\n---\n\n## 9. UNCERTAINTIES, CONFOUNDERS, AND ALTERNATIVE INTERPRETATIONS\n\n### 9.1 Key Uncertainties\n\n| Uncertainty | Risk | Mitigation |\n|-------------|------|------------|\n| Degree of *C. pallidicaule* susceptibility to *P. variabilis* isolates from quinoa | Quinoa-adapted isolates may be partially or fully avirulent on *C. pallidicaule* due to host-specific co-evolution. | Screen a large panel (15–20 isolates) from multiple hosts and geographic origins; prioritize *C. pallidicaule*-origin isolates. |\n| Maintainability of *P. variabilis* under controlled conditions | Obligate biotrophs can become attenuated or lose pathogenicity under prolonged greenhouse maintenance. | Regular re-isolation from field-collected material; comparative genomics with *Hyaloperonospora arabidopsidis* and *Phytophthora infestans*; long-read sequencing (PacBio/Nanopore). |\n| Non-host resistance in *C. pallidicaule* | The crop is reported to be \"quite resistant to most pests and diseases\"; verify identity by COX2 barcoding before each experiment. |\n| Environmental sensitivity of downy mildew | Temperature and humidity fluctuations can dramatically alter disease severity. | Use growth chambers or mist chambers with automated humidity control; include environmental monitoring (data loggers); run environmental controls in every experiment. |\n\n### 9.2 Confounders\n\n1. **Saponin content of *C. pallidicaule* seeds:** Seeds have high saponin content that may inhibit germination or act as natural antifungal/antibacterial agents. Surface sterilization may be required; germination rates should be compared between sterilized and non-sterilized seeds.\n\n2. **Quinoa as a living bridge:** Quinoa cv. 'Real' serves as the maintenance host for *P. variabilis*, but repeated transfers may select for isolates that are more quinoa-adapted than *C. pallidicaule*-adapted. Periodic re-isolation from *C. pallidicaule* is essential.\n\n3. **Propiconazole effects:** While propiconazole suppresses superimposed infections, it may have subtle effects on plant physiology or pathogen virulence. Control experiments without propiconazole should be run periodically.\n\n4. **Photoperiod and temperature effects on pathogenicity:** *P. variabilis* sporulation is light-dependent; short-day treatments may enhance sporulation. Temperature affects infection efficiency (optimum ~18–22°C). These variables must be standardized.\n\n5. **Polyploidy of quinoa vs. diploidy of *C. pallidicaule*:** Quinoa is an allotetraploid (AABB), while *C. pallidicaule* is a diploid (AA). The A-genome of *C. pallidicaule* is homeologous to the A-subgenome of quinoa, but gene dosage effects and missing B-subgenome genes may alter immune responses. This is a feature, not a bug — it provides a simplified genetic system for immune studies.\n\n### 9.3 Alternative Interpretations\n\n1. **If *B. cinerea* proves more compatible than *P. variabilis*:** The recommendation should shift to *B. cinerea* as primary, with *P. variabilis* demoted to complementary status. This would reflect the primacy of \"speed to establish\" — if the natural pathogen is difficult to maintain or assay, a well-tools-enabled generalist may be more productive overall.\n\n2. **If a novel *P. syringae* pathovar is discovered on *C. pallidicaule*:** This would elevate *P. syringae* to primary status, as the formal pathovar system and unmatched bacterial genetic tools would enable faster molecular dissection than *P. variabilis*. Research would shift to: (a) identifying biotic/abiotic factors that break resistance (e.g., soil microbiome, endophytes); (b) using *Agrobacterium*-mediated transient expression of pathogen effectors to test whether susceptibility can be engineered; (c) studying the resistance mechanisms themselves as the primary research objective.\n\n4. **The \"best\" pathovar may depend on the specific immune question:** Studying R-gene-mediated ETI requires an avirulent isolate (incompatible interaction); studying susceptibility requires a virulent isolate. VALIDATION / FALSIFICATION EXPERIMENTS\n\n### 10.1 Falsification of the Primary Recommendation\n\nThe hypothesis that \"*P. variabilis* is the best primary model pathogen for *C. pallidicaule*\" can be falsified by any of the following outcomes:\n\n**Falsification Experiment 1 — Cross-infection failure:**\n*Test:* Can *P. variabilis* isolates from quinoa consistently infect *C. pallidicaule* under controlled conditions?\n*Falsification criterion:* If >50% of *C. pallidicaule* accessions show no disease symptoms (score 0–1) when inoculated with the \"Kari\" isolate or *C. pallidicaule*-origin isolates at 1 × 10⁶ sporangia/mL, the premise that *P. variabilis* naturally infects the crop is called into question.\n*Contingency:* Shift to *B. cinerea* as primary.\n\n**Falsification Experiment 2 — Inability to maintain pathogen:**\n*Test:* Can *P. variabilis* be maintained on quinoa cv. 'Real' for >6 months without attenuation?\n*Falsification criterion:* If sporulation declines by >90% over three sequential transfers, or if the pathogen fails to produce disease on *C. pallidicaule* after prolonged greenhouse maintenance, the obligate biotrophic lifestyle becomes a liability.\n*Contingency:* Pursue *B. cinerea* and *P. syringae* as primary systems; maintain *P. variabilis* as a field-collected resource.\n\n**Falsification Experiment 3 — Superior alternative emerges:**\n*Test:* Does a more genetically tractable pathogen (e.g., a newly characterized *P. syringae* pathovar) prove compatible with *C. pallidicaule*?\n*Falsification criterion:* If *P. syringae* pv. *aptata* or a novel *P. syringae* pathovar causes robust disease with bacterial growth >10³-fold and produces clear lesions within 48 h, the formal pathovar system and bacterial genetic tools may outweigh the advantage of natural *P. variabilis* infection.\n*Contingency:* Elevate *P. syringae* to primary; retain *P. variabilis* as complementary biotroph model.\n\n### 10.2 Validation of the Recommended Approach\n\n**Validation Experiment 1 — Koch's postulates:**\n*Test:* Re-isolate the putative *P. variabilis* isolate from infected *C. pallidicaule* tissue and confirm identity by COX2 sequencing.\n*Success criterion:* The re-isolated pathogen must show ≥99% COX2 identity to the original isolate and must reproduce the same disease symptoms when re-inoculated onto quinoa cv. 'Real'.\n\n**Validation Experiment 2 — Reproducibility across laboratories:**\n*Test:* Share the designated working isolate (\"Isolate V\") with a collaborating laboratory in a different geographic region.\n*Success criterion:* Both laboratories achieve comparable AUDPC values (within ±20%) using the standardized protocol.\n\n**Validation Experiment 3 — Molecular detection at early time points:**\n*Test:* RT-PCR for *P. variabilis* COX2 at 2 dpi.\n*Success criterion:* Positive PCR at 2 dpi, confirming that infection is established before symptom appearance.\n\n---\n\n## 11. CONCLUSION\n\nThe establishment of a robust pathosystem in *Chenopodium pallidicaule* for deciphering plant immunity can be accomplished rapidly by exploiting a pathogen that **already naturally infects the crop**. *Peronospora variabilis*, the causal agent of quinoa downy mildew, meets this criterion definitively: it has been documented to infect three cañahua varieties in Bolivia, produces both compatible and incompatible interactions, and benefits from existing genetic resources in the quinoa–*P. variabilis* system. While it lacks the extensive genetic toolkit available for *Botrytis cinerea* or *Pseudomonas syringae*, its status as the most important quinoa disease, its documented virulence groups, and its conserved oomycete infection biology make it the most scientifically sound and temporally efficient choice.\n\nA multi-tiered strategy — *P. variabilis* as primary, *B. cinerea* as secondary necrotrophic model, and *P. syringae* as tertiary bacterial model — distributes risk, ensures that at least one pathosystem will be operational within months, and provides comprehensive coverage of plant immune mechanisms spanning PTI, ETI, SA-mediated biotroph resistance, and JA/ET-mediated necrotroph defense.\n\nThe \"pathovar\" question is resolved differently for each pathogen: for *P. variabilis*, we use \"isolate\" or \"virulence group\" and select the most aggressive, reproducible, and genetically distinguishable strain; for *P. syringae*, we leverage the formal >60-pathovar system; for *B. cinerea*, strain-level identification suffices. In all cases, the most suitable \"pathovar\" is the one that produces consistent, measurable disease on *C. pallidicaule* within the shortest timeframe, enabling the transition to molecular immune dissection.\n\n---\n\n## REFERENCES\n\n1. BACKGROUND: *Chenopodium pallidicaule* — Biology, Taxonomy, and Known Pathogens\n\n### 1.1 Taxonomy and Systematics\n\n*Chenopodium pallidicaule* Aellen (syn. *C. pallidum* Standl.) is a member of the family **Amaranthaceae** (formerly treated as Chenopodiaceae), subfamily Chenopodioideae. Its taxonomic position places it within the order Caryophyllales, making it closely related to quinoa, spinach, beets, and amaranths [1,2].\n\n| Rank | Classification |\n|------|----------------|\n| Kingdom | Plantae |\n| Clade | Tracheophytes, Angiosperms, Eudicots |\n| Order | Caryophyllales |\n| Family | Amaranthaceae |\n| Subfamily | Chenopodioideae |\n| Genus | *Chenopodium* |\n| Species | *C. pallidicaule* Aellen |\n| Genome | Diploid, 2n = 2x = 18 (A-genome) |\n\n**Key genomic fact**: The genome of *C. pallidicaule* (accession PI 478407) has been sequenced to chromosome-scale completeness (363 Mbp, N50 = 38.1 Mbp, 9 chromosomes) with 22,832 annotated gene models [3]. This diploid A-genome species is the simplest genetic system for studying the *Chenopodium* genus; it is the wild progenitor of the A subgenome of the allotetraploid quinoa (*C. quinoa*, AABB, 2n = 4x = 36) [3,4].\n\n### 1.2 Native Range, Cultivation, and Ecological Adaptation\n\n*C. pallidicaule* (commonly called cañihua, kañiwa, or kanawa) is native to the high Andes of Peru, Bolivia, Ecuador, Chile, and Argentina, where it has been cultivated for over 3,000 years [5,6]. It thrives at altitudes of 2,500–4,000 m above sea level and is exceptionally tolerant to frost, drought, and saline-alkaline soils. It is a **facultative halophyte**, capable of growing at electrical conductivity values up to 12–16 dS/m [7]. Establishing robust model pathosystems within *Chenopodium quinoa* (and related species such as *C. pallidicaule*) requires knowledge of which pathogens naturally infect quinoa, which produce measurable compatible or incompatible interactions, and which are experimentally tractable.\n\nBelow I survey the major fungal, oomycete, and bacterial pathogens that have been documented on quinoa, with emphasis on those for which controlled infection studies have been performed. Proposed Model Pathogen: *Peronospora variabilis* (Gaum.) 1919\n\n### 1.1 Rationale and Justification\n\nI propose **Peronospora variabilis**, the obligate biotrophic oomycete that causes downy mildew of quinoa and cañahua (C. pallidicaule), as the primary model pathogen for dissecting plant immunity in this novel halophytic crop. The justification rests on the following criteria:\n\n#### A. Natural Host–Pathogen Compatibility (Host Specificity)\n\n*P. variabilis* is the **co-evolved, natural pathogen** of *Chenopodium* species. It was previously classified as *Peronospora farinosa* f. sp. *chenopodii* before being recognized as a distinct species (Byford 1970; Thines et al. 2009). Critically, its infection of *C. pallidicaule* has been **formally confirmed**: the first report of *P. variabilis* causing downy mildew in cañahua (*C. pallidicaule*) in Bolivia demonstrated that three cañahua varieties were infected and developed characteristic disease symptoms, with pathogen identity confirmed by PCR and Sanger sequencing of the COX2 region (Rollano-Peñaloza et al., submitted to *Plant Disease*, 2021). The pathogen exhibits **stringent host specificity** within the Chenopodieae tribe (Nolen et al. 2022, *Plant Disease* 106:1382–1391); it does not infect non-host plants outside this group, which is an advantage because it minimizes confounding interactions with secondary pathogens and focuses the immune response on a single, well-adapted biotroph.\n\n#### B. Biological Parallels to the Hpa–*Arabidopsis* Model System\n\n*P. variabilis* belongs to the family Peronosporaceae, order Peronosporales—the same group that contains **Hyaloperonospora arabidopsidis** (Hpa), the most extensively studied obligate biotroph in molecular plant pathology. Context and Strategic Considerations\n\n*Chenopodium pallidicaule* Aellen (kañihua/cañihua, 2n = 2x = 18) is a halophytic grain crop native to the Andean altiplano, closely related to the allotetraploid quinoa (*C. quinoa*, 2n = 4x = 36). Its genome has been sequenced (Mangelson et al., 2019, *Plant Biotechnology Journal*), and it serves as the putative A-genome progenitor of quinoa. Let me write a comprehensive, well-structured answer.","calls":[],"responses":[],"answer":"# Establishing a Robust Pathosystem for *Chenopodium pallidicaule* to Study Plant Immunity\n\n---\n\n## 1. Documented Diseases and Pathogens of *Chenopodium pallidicaule*\n\n### 1.1 Direct Reports on *C. pallidicaule*\n\nThe literature on diseases specifically affecting *Chenopodium pallidicaule* (cañihua, kañihua, paico) is sparse, reflecting the crop's under-studied status. The most significant confirmed pathogen is:\n\n**Peronospora variabilis** (oomycete, downy mildew) — First formally reported on *C. pallidicaule* in Bolivia by Rollano-Peñaloza et al. (2021) [*Pathogens* 10(4), 469; also *Plant Disease* 2021]. Symptomatic plants showed upper-leaf chlorosis and heavy sporulation on the abaxial surface. Artificial inoculation of three cañahua varieties reproduced the disease, and pathogen identity was confirmed by PCR and Sanger sequencing of PvCox2 (99.8% identity to *P. variabilis* from quinoa) and PvITS (100% identity). This pathogen is an **obligate biotroph**, cannot be cultured axenically, and causes yield losses of 35–100% in quinoa. It represents the most economically important disease but has **limited genetic tools** (no sequenced genome, no transformation system), making it a challenging \"model\" pathogen for mechanistic immune studies.\n\nA Peruvian survey of cañihua fields in the Andean Altiplano (ResearchGate, 2022) confirmed *Peronospora* sp. as the main pathology occurring during the agricultural season. No other fungal, bacterial, or viral diseases have been formally described exclusively on *C. pallidicaule*.\n\n### 1.2 Pathogens of Related *Chenopodium* Species (Relevant Proxies)\n\nGiven the close taxonomic relationship between *C. pallidicaule* (diploid, 2n=2x=18) and quinoa (*C. quinoa*, tetraploid, 2n=4x=36), pathogens of quinoa are highly likely to infect *C. pallidicaule*. The comprehensive review by Colque-Little et al. The ideal pathosystem requires: (i) a pathogen that naturally infects *C. pallidicaule*, (ii) well-characterized virulence/avirulence factors, (iii) genetic tools for the pathogen, (iv) a short infection cycle amenable to controlled-environment assays, and (v) quantifiable host resistance/susceptibility scales. Below I propose and justify the selection of **Peronospora variabilis Gäum.** (an obligate biotrophic oomycete) as the primary model pathogen, with detailed protocols for screening virulence, determining the most suitable pathovar/race, and executing the experimental program.\n\n---\n\n## 2. Selection of the Model Pathogen: *Peronospora variabilis*\n\n### 2.1 Biological and Taxonomic Rationale\n\n*Peronospora variabilis* is the causal agent of downy mildew on quinoa (*Chenopodium quinoa* Willd.) and white goosefoot (*Chenopodium album* L.). Crucially, **Rollano-Peñaloza et al. (2021)** reported the first confirmation of *P. variabilis* infecting *C. pallidicaule* in Bolivia. Let me write a comprehensive, detailed answer to each of the 8 questions.","calls":[],"responses":[],"answer":"# *Peronospora variabilis* Pathosystem: Comprehensive Analysis for Genetic Model Potential\n\n---\n\n## (1) The Four Virulence Groups (V1–V4) and Resistance Factors (R1–R3)\n\nThe foundational study by **Ochoa, Frinking & Jacobs (1999)** used 20 *P. variabilis* isolates collected from quinoa fields across Ecuador (south, central, and north regions) and 60 quinoa lines to delineate the pathogen's genetic structure. Using a postulation (differential infection) approach, they identified **four virulence groups (V1–V4)** and **three host resistance factors (R1–R3)**. The key findings:\n\n### Virulence Group Definitions\n\n| Virulence Group | Representative Isolates | Virulence Profile | Geographic Distribution (Ecuador) |\n|:--|:--|:--|:--|\n| **V1** | Isolate 18 | Least virulent; basal race | Found in northern regions |\n| **V2** | Isolates 1, 4, 22, 23 | Overcomes V1 | South only |\n| **V3** | Isolates 20, 21 | Overcomes V1 + V2 | Northern regions |\n| **V4** | Isolates 10, 12, 14, 2 | Overcomes V1 + V2 + V3; **no known resistance** | Central region only |\n\n### Resistance Factor Mappings\n\n| Resistance Factor | Quinoa Lines Carrying It | Resists Which Virulence Group(s) |\n|:--|:--|:--|\n| **R1** | ECU-621, ECU-262; also Faro, Bordeaux, Otavalo 4, Tunkahuan | V1 only |\n| **R2** | Ingapirca (cultivar), ECU-470 | V1 and V2 |\n| **R3** | Inagrofa, Masal 3-89-7E, Colorado, ECU-223, Amarilla de Olmedo, Masal 3-89-5e1E | V1, V2, and V3 |\n\n**Critical finding:** No quinoa line tested (including 29 that showed mixed reactions) exhibited resistance to **V4 isolates**. This makes V4 the most aggressive and economically dangerous virulence group—it overcomes all known resistance factors. Ochoa et al. INTRODUCTION AND STRATEGIC RATIONALE\n\n### 2.1 The Case for *Chenopodium pallidicaule*\n\n*Chenopodium pallidicaule* Aellen (cañahua, kañawa; 2n = 2x = 18) is a semi-domesticated Andean crop highly tolerant to frost, drought, and saline soils, cultivated at 3,600–4,400 m a.s.l. in the Bolivian and Peruvian Altiplano (Mangelson et al., 2019). Its diploid genome (~363 Mbp, 22,832 annotated gene models) has been sequenced and chromosome-scale assembled, revealing strong synteny with the A-subgenome of allotetraploid quinoa (*C. quinoa*, AABB, 2n = 4x = 36). This positions *C. pallidicaule* as an **ideal simplified genetic model** for studying gene function in the Amaranthaceae. Despite its agricultural potential, the crop's immune system and disease resistance mechanisms remain profoundly understudied, representing a critical knowledge gap as climate change drives the expansion of crop cultivation into new environments where biotic stresses may intensify.\n\n### 2.2 Why a Model Pathosystem Is Needed\n\nDeciphering plant immunity requires well-characterized, genetically tractable pathosystems—reciprocal interactions between a host and its pathogen in which both partners have tools available for molecular manipulation. Biotrophic pathogens such as downy mildews are particularly valuable for studying these layers because they must maintain living host tissue, forcing sustained immune engagement. The *Arabidopsis*–*Hyaloperonospora arabidopsidis* pathosystem exemplifies how such systems yield deep mechanistic insights (Baxter et al., 2010).\n\n### 2.3 Objectives\n\n1. INTRODUCTION: THE CASE FOR *Chenopodium pallidicaule* AS A MODEL HALOPYTIC CROP\n\n### 1.1 Biological and Taxonomic Context\n\n*Chenopodium pallidicaule* Aellen (cañahua/cañihua/kañawa), a semi-domesticated Andean crop, belongs to the genus *Chenopodium* within the family Amaranthaceae (subfamily Chenopodioideae; formerly Chenopodiaceae). It is a diploid species with **2n = 2x = 18 chromosomes**, making it a simplified genetic relative of the allotetraploid quinoa (*C. quinoa*, AABB, 2n = 4x = 36) [Mangelson et al., 2019]. The genome of *C. pallidicaule* (~363 Mbp, 22,832 annotated gene models) has been sequenced and chromosome-scale assembled, confirming strong synteny with the A-subgenome of quinoa [Mangelson et al., 2019]. This diploidy, combined with its close relationship to the economically more important quinoa, positions *C. pallidicaule* as an **ideal simplified genetic model** for studying gene function in the Amaranthaceae.\n\nThe crop is native to the Bolivian Peruvian Altiplano, where it is cultivated at 3,600–4,400 m a.s.l. It is highly tolerant to frost, drought, and saline soils. Importantly, it is **generally reported as resistant to most pests and diseases**, though this resistance profile is understudied scientifically [Repo-Carrasco et al., 2003; PFAF].\n\n### 1.2 Known Pathogens of *C. pallidicaule*\n\nA targeted literature search reveals the following confirmed or suspected pathogens:\n\n| Pathogen | Type | Host specificity | Reference |\n|----------|------|------------------|-----------|\n| ***Peronospora variabilis*** (Gäum.) | Oomycete (biotroph) | Limited to *Chenopodium* spp.; infects *C. quinoa*, *C. album*, *C. murale*, *C. hybridum*, and now confirmed on *C. pallidicaule* | Rollano-Peñaloza et al. (2021); Colque-Little et al. This pathogen is **confirmed to infect *C. pallidicaule*** under greenhouse conditions, displays a short infection cycle (9–11 days to visible symptoms and sporulation), is amenable to rapid artificial inoculation, and has an existing foundation of virulence groups and resistance factors that can be leveraged. Let me compose it.","calls":[],"responses":[],"answer":"# Establishing a Robust Pathosystem for *Chenopodium pallidicaule* to Decipher Plant Immunity\n\n---\n\n## 1. Proposed Model Pathogen and Justification\n\n### Primary Recommendation: *Peronospora variabilis* Gäum. (Oomycete, Downy Mildew)\n\nI propose **Peronospora variabilis** as the primary model pathogen for establishing a fast, robust pathosystem in *Chenopodium pallidicaule*. The justification rests on six pillars:\n\n#### 1.1 Natural Host–Pathogen Compatibility Confirmed\n*P. variabilis* is an obligate biotrophic oomycete that causes downy mildew on quinoa (*C. quinoa*) and several *Chenopodium* spp. Critically, **natural infection of *C. pallidicaule* (cañahua/cañihua) by *P. variabilis* has been formally reported** in Bolivia, with pathogenicity confirmed by artificial inoculation of three cañahua varieties and molecular identification via PCR amplification of the PvCox2 and PvITS regions (Fondevilla et al., 2023; Rollano-Peñaloza et al., 2022). This means the basic host–pathogen compatibility already exists—no need to wait for fortuitous natural emergence or laborious cross-host transmission experiments.\n\n#### 1.2 A Partially Characterized Pre-existing Pathosystem in the Close Relative Quinoa\nThe *C. quinoa* – *P. variabilis* pathosystem is the best-studied disease system in this crop complex:\n- **Four virulence groups (V1–V4)** and **three resistance factors (R1, R2, R3)** were postulated by Ochoa et al. (1999) using 20 isolates and 60 Ecuadorian quinoa lines. A differential set of four quinoa lines (ECU-288 [susceptible check], ECU-291 [R1], ECU-270 [R2], ECU-379 [R3]) enables classification of isolates into virulence groups.\n- High genetic variation for disease severity (5–83%), sporulation (0.2–83.6%), and incidence (36.8–92%) has been documented across 132 genotypes, with high heritability estimates (severity: 0.72–0.78; sporulation: 0.78–0.82) (Colque-Little et al., 2021).\n- A set of reference cultivars (Puno, Titicaca, Vikinga, Real, Kurmi) with known susceptib  …[+29554]"}]}]},{"label":"Run 4","awarded":5.5,"total":10.0,"report":"# Establishing a Robust Pathosystem in *Chenopodium pallidicaule* for Deciphering Plant Immunity\n\n## Model Pathogen Selection, Virulence Screening, and Pathovar Determination\n\n---\n\n## EXECUTIVE SUMMARY\n\n**Primary model pathogen recommendation:** ***Peronospora variabilis*** Gäum. (oomycete, Peronosporaceae), the causal agent of quinoa downy mildew, is the most suitable primary model pathogen for establishing a rapid, robust pathosystem in *Chenopodium pallidicaule* Aellen. This recommendation is grounded in the single most critical criterion for speed: ***P. variabilis* is the only candidate pathogen for which natural infection of *C. pallidicaule* has been experimentally documented** (Rollano-Peñaloza et al., 2021). The pathogen infects three cañahua varieties, produces classic downy mildew symptoms, and its identity was confirmed by PCR and Sanger sequencing. Furthermore, *P. variabilis* supports both compatible (susceptible cultivar 'Real') and incompatible (hypersensitive response in cultivar 'Bol 1.1'; tolerant cultivar 'Kurmi') interactions, providing the dual readout essential for immune dissection. Four virulence groups and three resistance factors have already been characterized (Ochoa et al., 1999), providing an immediate framework for pathotyping.\n\n**Complementary systems:** *Botrytis cinerea* (necrotrophic ascomycete with world-class genetic tools) and *Pseudomonas syringae* pv. *aptata* (bacterial hemibiotroph with a formal pathovar system and natural Chenopodiaceae affinity) are recommended as secondary and tertiary models, respectively.\n\n**Timeline to robust pathosystem:** ~14–16 weeks from isolate acquisition to a validated, reproducible protocol, with molecular dissection extending to 12 months.\n\n**Key operational definition:** For *P. variabilis*, the equivalent of \"pathovar\" is **\"isolate\"** or **\"virulence group\"** — no formal formae speciales or pathovars have been described within this oomycete species. The selection process therefore focuses on identifying the most aggressive, genetically distinguishable, and reproducible isolate(s) for experimental use.\n\n---\n\n## 1. INTRODUCTION\n\n### 1.1 The Crop and the Challenge\n\n*Chenopodium pallidicaule* Aellen (cañihua/kañihua, 2n = 2x = 18, genome size ~363 Mbp with 22,832 annotated gene models; Mangelson et al., 2019), is a halophytic diploid member of the family Amaranthaceae (subfamily Chenopodioideae, formerly Chenopodiaceae). It is a semi-domesticated Andean pseudocereal closely related to the allotetraploid quinoa (*C. quinoa*, AABB, 2n = 4x = 36). *C. pallidicaule* possesses exceptional stress-tolerance traits — frost, drought, and saline soil tolerance — making it a prime candidate for climate-resilient crop production. However, its systematic deployment to new environments will expose the crop to novel biotic pressures, including adapted pathogens from related *Chenopodium* species and generalist pathogens from adjacent ecosystems. Critically, it naturally infects the closest relative of *C. pallidicaule* — **common lambsquarters, *Chenopodium album***. A recent transcriptome study (Zhu et al., 2025, *Genes* 13:2177) demonstrated that *B. cinerea* strain HZ‑011, isolated from *Rumex patientia* (Amaranthaceae), causes progressive necrotic lesions on *C. album*, suppresses photosynthetic gene expression, and kills the plant within 5 days post-inoculation. This provides direct evidence that *B. cinerea* can recognize, infect, and kill a *Chenopodium* host.\n\n#### (b) Rapid, Measurable Disease Cycle\n*B. cinerea* produces visible lesions within **24–48 hours** on susceptible tissue and reaches maximal size by **3–5 days**. Lesion diameter can be quantified with simple image-analysis software (e.g., ImageJ). This speed is essential for the \"as quickly as possible\" mandate.\n\n#### (c) Effortless Culture and Inoculum Production\nThe fungus grows luxuriantly on plain agar (PDA, OA, or WPM) at 20–25 °C with diffuse light. Abundant conidia are produced within 7–14 days. Spores can be harvested in sterile water containing 0.01 % Tween‑20, filtered, counted with a hemocytometer, and adjusted to any required concentration. Let me structure it comprehensively.","calls":[],"responses":[],"answer":"# Establishing a Robust Pathosystem in *Chenopodium pallidicaule* for Plant Immunity Research\n\n## 1. Proposed Model Pathogen: *Pseudomonas syringae* (Bacterial Leaf Spot)\n\n### 1.1 Justification\n\nI propose the **_Pseudomonas syringae_ pathovars group** as the model pathogen system for dissecting plant immunity in *Chenopodium pallidicaule*. This recommendation rests on four pillars:\n\n| Criterion | *P. syringae* advantage | Evidence |\n|-----------|------------------------|----------|\n| **Genetic tools** | Fully sequenced genomes for >20 pathovars; transposon mutagenesis libraries; effector-deletion mutants (e.g., DC3000Δ28E lacking all 28 T3 effectors); Agrobacterium-mediated transformation | Xin & He (2013) *Annu Rev Phytopathol*; Baltrus et al. (2011) *PLoS Pathog* |\n| **Pathovar diversity** | >60 validly published pathovars with distinct host ranges spanning >180 plant species, including Chenopodiaceae | Lindeberg et al. (2009) *Mol Plant Pathol*; Wikipedia *P. syringae* list |\n| **Molecular mechanistic depth** | Two-tiered immune recognition (PTI/ETI) first decoded in this system; type III secretion system (T3SS) and ~28–30 effectors characterized; phytotoxin coronatine understood at structural level | Xin et al. (2013) *Annu Rev Phytopathol*; Dodds & Rathjen (2010) *Annu Rev Biochem* |\n| **Practicality** | Easy axenic culture (NGM/YEP agar, 28 °C); short incubation (lesions in 48–72 h); BSL‑1; can be propagated on *Nicotiana benthamiana* or *C. pallidicaule* without special facilities | Standard protocols; Macan et al. (2022) *Methods Mol Biol* |\n\n**Key point:** *P. syringae* pv. *aptata* is a natural bacterial leaf spot pathogen of beet and Swiss chard (*Beta vulgaris*, Amaranthaceae subfam. Chenopodioideae), making it the only formally named pathovar with documented affinity for our crop’s botanical family. ## A Broader Principle: Simple Interface, Broad Function

The single tool is one instance of a wider principle: <strong>keep the tool interface narrow, and let it map onto broad function</strong>. Narrow is not the same as limited, it means the surface the model calls through is small, while the function reachable behind it stays wide.

<div class="sw-banner sw-reveal">
  <span class="sw-kicker">Design principle</span>
  <h3>More tools do not mean more reach</h3>
  <p>Every additional tool schema is one more thing the model must read, distinguish from the others, and choose between, overhead that competes with the task itself. A single interface the model already knows how to drive frees it to reason about <em>how to compose function</em> for the task, rather than <em>which tool to pick</em>.</p>
  <p>The pattern recurs across agent designs: a coding agent needs little more than a <strong>terminal</strong>, build, test, edit, inspect, install; a browser agent reaches a wide range of web function through the <strong>browser</strong> alone. The interface is narrow; the function behind it is wide. UniSwarm applies this to orchestration: <strong>one dispatch tool</strong>, with every mode of work expressed through how it is called.</p>
</div>

In practice the better question is not which tool to add, but how to abstract broader function behind the tools already present, without growing the count, and sometimes by shrinking it. That is how reach is balanced against the difficulty of use.

<script>
(function() {
    // scroll-reveal
    const items = document.querySelectorAll(".sw-reveal");
    if ("IntersectionObserver" in window) {
        const io = new IntersectionObserver((entries) => {
            entries.forEach((e) => { if (e.isIntersecting) { e.target.classList.add("is-visible"); io.unobserve(e.target); } });
        }, { threshold: 0.12 });
        items.forEach((el) => io.observe(el));
    } else {
        items.forEach((el) => el.classList.add("is-visible"));
    }

    // floating TOC
    const toc = document.getElementById("sw-toc");
    const toggle = document.getElementById("sw-toc-toggle");
    const bar = document.getElementById("sw-toc-prog-bar");
    if (toggle && toc) toggle.addEventListener("click", () => toc.classList.toggle("collapsed"));

    const links = Array.from(document.querySelectorAll(".sw-toc-list a"));
    const secs = links.map((a) => {
        const id = a.getAttribute("href").slice(1);
        return { a, el: document.getElementById(id) };
    }).filter((s) => s.el);

    const onScroll = () => {
        if (bar) {
            const docH = document.documentElement.scrollHeight - window.innerHeight;
            bar.style.width = Math.min(100, Math.max(0, (window.scrollY / (docH || 1)) * 100)) + "%";
        }
        const pos = window.scrollY + 160;
        let active = secs.length ? secs[0] : null;
        for (const s of secs) { if (s.el.offsetTop <= pos) active = s; }
        links.forEach((l) => l.classList.remove("active"));
        if (active) active.a.classList.add("active");
    };
    window.addEventListener("scroll", onScroll, { passive: true });
    onScroll();
})();
</script>
